# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

## Local Chrome

The default daemon can keep many tabs and visit many sites; browser-use has
no per-site, screenshot, or result-count limit that requires a new daemon.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

The default daemon can keep many tabs and visit many sites; browser-use has
no per-site, screenshot, or result-count limit that requires a new daemon.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

15	    14	# Classify Every Exercise as Competitive, Special Preparatory or General Preparatory Before Placing It in a Phase
16	    15	
17	    16	**What it is** — The paragraph that closes 8.3 sits on PDF 444 / p.433 above the 8.4 heading, and leads straight into it. The authors say exercises "may be divided into three broad categories for most sports": *Competitive Exercises*, "exercises that are actually performed in competition"; *Special Physical Preparation exercises*, which "may be similar to the competitive movements or largely dissimilar exercises that may develop the specific motor qualities required in the sport"; and *General Physical Preparation exercises*, "usually different from the competition movements in type, pattern, mode of execution and speed, and ... intended for general development to form a foundation for later stages of training" (PDF 444 / p.433, checked against the page image). Section 8.4.1 then gives the Russian source. In Russia "not only is all training broadly divided into general preparatory, special preparatory and competitive phases, but all exercises are classified similarly," a practice the authors credit to A Novikov (1949), who held that classification is "the most important foundation for education and training" (PDF 444). They quote Matveyev, in "revised excerpts" from the English translation of *The Fundamentals of Sports Training* (1981): the key distinction is an exercise's "similarity or difference compared with the specific movements characterising a given sport," which splits exercises "into *competition* and *preparatory* exercises, then into *special preparatory* and *general preparatory* exercises." Competition exercises are "performed in the same way as during competition." Special preparatory exercises "consist of elements of the competition actions and variations of them, as well as actions similar to them, in terms of the form and the character of the abilities displayed," and divide into *preliminary exercises* "(to help the athlete master the movement)" and *developmental exercises* "(to develop physical qualities)" (Matveyev, quoted on PDF 444 / p.433).
18	    17	
19	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' claim: "The ability to place all exercises (and the different techniques of using them) into these categories enables one to avoid making any serious errors in selecting any of them to achieve a specific training purpose at a given stage of a periodisation scheme" (PDF 444 / p.433). Matveyev's reason for keeping competition exercises in training: without them "it is impossible to fully equip the athlete with the specific requirements of the given sport, and stimulate the development of specific preparedness" (PDF 444). Inference: the classification works as a filter because each class has a different job, so a mismatch between the class and the phase is visible before the session is run.
20	    19	
21	    20	**When to apply** — When building a phase or auditing a programme, tag each exercise (and each way of using it, since the authors include "the different techniques of using them") with its class, and check that the mix fits the phase. Matveyev notes that preliminary and developmental exercises "are introduced at the different stages of training in unequal proportions" (PDF 444). Eric's review: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: Eric's four-step spectrum matches Matveyev's tree if "specific preparation" is read as the preliminary subtype and "specific development" as the developmental subtype; the book gives Matveyev's subtypes, not Bondarchuk's four classes.
22	    21	
23	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The classification is presented as a Russian convention with no data on whether using it reduces selection errors; "avoid making any serious errors" is the authors' assertion. The boundary between special and general preparatory is loose in the book's own wording: a special preparatory exercise may be "largely dissimilar" to the competition movement (PDF 444), so similarity of form alone does not decide the class. The authors elsewhere warn that GPP and SPP can merge (see [[heuristic--gpp-and-spp-form-one-unit-curtail-gpp-for-advanced-athletes]]). The Matveyev text is a revised excerpt, so exact wording may be the authors' edit rather than the translation.
24	    23	
25	    24	**Example** — Inference, built from the categories: in a sprinter's programme, the sprint race is competitive; resisted sprints and starts are special preparatory, with technique drills as preliminary and sled pulls as developmental; back squats and general circuits are general preparatory. The book's own worked case is weightlifting (8.4.2, PDF 445 / p.434), where the snatch and clean and jerk are Group 1, auxiliary lifts Group 2, and general physical training Group 3 (see [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]]).
26	    25	
27	    26	**Related** — [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] (Bondarchuk splits the special group into specialized-preparatory and specialized-developmental classes; Matveyev keeps one special preparatory group with two subtypes. Different taxonomies, not a conflict), [[heuristic--general-preparatory-exercises-three-functions-and-two-selection-rules]], [[framework--matveyev-categorisation-of-competitive-exercises-table-8-2]], [[framework--general-and-specific-components-of-a-training-programme]], [[heuristic--dynamic-correspondence-means-matching-motor-characteristics-not-copying-the-sport-movement]], [[heuristic--gpp-and-spp-form-one-unit-curtail-gpp-for-advanced-athletes]]

42	    14	# Choose General Preparatory Exercises for Three Jobs, Limited by Time and Equipment, and Shaped by the Sport
43	    15	
44	    16	**What it is** — In the Matveyev excerpt the authors quote, general preparatory exercises are "the fundamental, practical means to achieve the athlete's general preparation." They are "much broader in scope and more varied than the other groups," and their list "is theoretically unlimited, though practically their use is restricted by the time which can be taken without detriment from other means of training and by the availability of equipment" (PDF 444 / p.433, checked against the page image). Two selection requirements: "Firstly, the athlete must have a comprehensive background of multi-faceted physical education. Secondly, the contents of the athlete's general preparation should reflect the specifics of the sport." Three functions: "(a) to form, strengthen or restore motor skills which play an auxiliary, facilitatory role in sport perfecting (b) to teach abilities developed insufficiently by the given sport, increase the general work capacity or preserve it (c) to provide active rest, promote restoration after strenuous loading and counteract the monotony of training" (PDF 445 / p.434, checked against the page image).
45	    17	
46	    18	**Why it works** — Matveyev's statement is that "These functions define the role of the general preparatory exercises in the athlete's training programme" (PDF 445). Inference: each function names a gap the sport itself does not fill (auxiliary skills, neglected abilities, recovery and variety), so a general exercise earns its place by filling one of those gaps, not by being "general."
47	    19	
48	    20	**When to apply** — When deciding whether a general exercise belongs in the plan, name which of (a), (b) or (c) it serves, check it against the time cost "without detriment from other means," and check that it still "reflect[s] the specifics of the sport." Function (c) matches the authors' restorative use of GPP in the concentrated-loading models (see [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]]). Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: function (c) is a load-design route to recovery, so it fits that stance without adding a recovery modality.
49	    21	
50	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The list is Matveyev's classification, not a tested rule; no data are given on which functions matter most. The first requirement assumes an athlete who already has "a comprehensive background of multi-faceted physical education"; Inference: with a poorly prepared athlete the order reverses, and building that background becomes the job of the general work itself. The authors elsewhere say standard GPP should be curtailed for advanced athletes (see [[heuristic--gpp-and-spp-form-one-unit-curtail-gpp-for-advanced-athletes]]), so "theoretically unlimited" is not a licence to expand GPP.
51	    23	
52	    24	**Example** — The book's weightlifting case (8.4.2): general preparatory exercises for lifters are drawn from ten disciplines, including track and field ("Acceleration runs: 400 - 1000 meters," jumps, throws, "cross-country running 1-3 km"), gymnastics, sport games, cycling, rowing, swimming, winter sports and hiking, with gymnastics, acrobatics, mobility games, skating and middle-distance running named as appropriate for juveniles (PDF 447 / p.436, checked against the page image).
53	    25	
54	    26	**Related** — [[framework--competition-special-preparatory-and-general-preparatory-exercise-classes]], [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]], [[principle--minimax-principle-of-training-economics]] (the time-cost limit), [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]

69	    14	# Matveyev's Table 8.2: Competitive Exercises Grouped as Monostructural, Polystructural or Complexes
70	    15	
71	    16	**What it is** — The authors present Matveyev's "classification of competitive exercises" as a further illustration of "the meticulous attention to detail used in the Russian system" (PDF 445 / p.434). Table 8.2, "Categorisation of Competitive Exercises in Different Types of Sport," read from the page image, has three overall groupings:
72	    17	- *Monostructural Exercises (relatively stable forms)*: 1. Speed and Strength Exercises (A. Jumps; B. Throws (Shot, javelin, etc); C. Lifting weights; D. Sprint); 2. Cyclic Endurance (A. High intensity endurance events; B. Low and medium intensity endurance).
73	    18	- *Polystructural Exercises (variable forms)*: 1. Team Games (A. High intensity interval; B. Prolonged relatively continuous); 2. Sporting Combat (A. Non physical contact (fencing etc); B. Physical Contact (boxing, wrestling etc)).
74	    19	- *Complexes of Exercises*: 1. Dual and Combined Events with a stable content (A. Homogeneous Two-event & Combined events (skating 4-events, Alpine 3-events etc); B. Non-homogeneous dual and combined events (decathlon, pentathlon, ski dual etc)); 2. Dual and Combined Events with a periodically renewed content (A. Aesthetic Sports (gymnastics, diving, skating, acrobatics etc)).
75	    20	
76	    21	**Why it works** — The book gives the table without a stated rationale. Inference: the top split is by how stable the movement form is (fixed versus variable versus a set of events), and the second split is by the dominant quality or contact demand, which are the features that decide how specific the special preparatory work can be.
77	    22	
78	    23	**When to apply** — As a first sort when a coach meets an unfamiliar sport: place it in a cell, then borrow programming from neighbours in that cell. Inference: American football sits under Polystructural, Team Games, A (high intensity interval), the same cell as other field sports with repeated short efforts.
79	    24	
80	    25	**When NOT to apply** — The table carries no data and no stated purpose beyond illustration. Some cells are thin: Dual and Combined Events "with a periodically renewed content" has a single subgroup, aesthetic sports. Skating appears both in the homogeneous combined events and among aesthetic sports, so a sport can fall in more than one cell. The 6.7 classification by Farfel (acyclic, cyclic, complex) cuts the same sports differently, by movement organisation and energy supply (see [[framework--three-sport-groups-acyclic-cyclic-complex-for-programming]]); the two schemes are different lenses, not a conflict. Note the book reuses the label "Table 8.2" on PDF 453 / p.442 for the A/B overtraining comparison, which is printed as Table 8.3 on PDF 454.
81	    26	
82	    27	**Example** — The table's own placements: sprint and weightlifting are monostructural speed-strength exercises, while boxing and wrestling are polystructural combat with physical contact (PDF 445 / p.434, checked against the page image).
83	    28

99	    14	# Medvedev's Weightlifting Classification: Competition, Special Preparatory and General Groups, Recast as 12 Fundamental and 4 Additional Means
100	    15	
101	    16	**What it is** — The authors offer the Russian weightlifting scheme as a model that "may then be applied in any other sport" (PDF 445 / p.434). Per Medvedev (1986): "Group 1 consists of the competition exercises (in weightlifting, the Snatch and Clean & Jerk)"; "Group 2 combines the Special Preparatory exercises," subdivided into auxiliary snatch exercises, auxiliary clean and jerk exercises, and "auxiliary exercises for the legs, back, (torso), arms and shoulder girdle"; "Group 3 consists of General Preparatory exercises" (PDF 445, checked against the page image). The passage that follows, presented under Medvedev's classification, then regroups them by effect. Group 1 "combines the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means," mostly "in conformity with the technique of the classic Snatch and classic Clean & Jerk," lifted heavy "at great power," so it is "the fundamental group." Group 2 holds the "special preparatory (developmental) exercises," which "for the most part ... have a local effect," use "relatively light weights," develop "relatively small" power and "can be significantly different in technique" (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). "The fundamental exercises are divided into 12 groups and the additional exercises into 4 groups" (PDF 446 / p.435): fundamental 1-12 are classic snatch, squat snatch, power snatch, snatch pull, classic clean and jerk, squat clean, jerk, power clean, clean pull, barbell squats, good mornings and pressing; additional 13-16 are leg exercises, back exercises, arm and shoulder girdle exercises, and "The Snatch and Clean & Jerk Exercises with weights less than 60%" (PDF 446, checked against the page image).
102	    17	
103	    18	**Why it works** — The stated reason for the regrouping: all exercises, "depending on their coordination structure, method of training and amount of resistance," develop physical qualities and contribute to "the perfecting of technical mastery" to different extents, so "it is appropriate to divide all of the exercises of the first and second groups into two independent parts" (PDF 445 / p.434). Inference: the split sorts exercises by the size of the training effect they carry, so that heavy, technique-matched lifting can be tracked apart from light local work.
104	    19	
105	    20	**When to apply** — When building a classification for a sport's own exercise pool, use the two passes the book models: first by resemblance (competition, special, general), then by effect (fundamental versus additional). Inference: the clean, jerk and squat variants Eric names as core work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104) would sit in the fundamental group; single-joint assistance work would be additional.
106	    21	
107	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is weightlifting-specific and the book reports no outcome data for it. The source is internally loose: Group 1 is first "the competition exercises" and then "the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means" (PDF 445), and the light snatch and clean and jerk under 60% move to the additional group. The numbered list of "One hundred different weightlifting exercises" that follows (PDF 447-449 / p.436-438) uses its own group numbering, which jumps from Group 7 to Group 9 with no Group 8 heading (PDF 448 / p.437), and has no entry for the under-60% group. The 100-exercise list itself is not atomized here.
108	    23	
109	    24	**Example** — Pull variants show how one fundamental group expands in the 100-exercise list: snatch pulls from the floor, from below, at and above the knee, from a block, "with four, 3-second stops (at the instant of starting lift, at knees, above the knees, heels raised)," slow then fast, and combined with the full snatch (items 15-28, PDF 447-448 / p.436-437, checked against the page images).
110	    25

126	    14	# Count Fundamental and Additional Training Loads Separately, Not as One Total
127	    15	
128	    16	**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification the book presents under Medvedev (1986): "in order to more objectively assess the training influence, the athlete is subjected to exercises from Group 1, their loading is counted as fundamental, while the loading in the Group 2 is considered additional. Finally, it is important that *fundamental and additional training loads should be calculated and analysed separately*" (PDF 446 / p.435, italics in the original, checked against the page image).
129	    17	
130	    18	**Why it works** — The passage's reasoning: Group 1 lifts are heavy, close to competition technique and done "at great power," while Group 2 lifts are light, local and develop "relatively small" power (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). Inference: one tonnage total would let a large volume of light local work mask a drop in heavy competition-pattern work, or the reverse, so the two need separate columns to show what the athlete actually did.
131	    19	
132	    20	**When to apply** — In any training log that sums volume (lifts, tonnage, reps above a percentage), keep at least two totals: the core lifts that carry the main training effect, and the assistance work. Inference: in a team setting this is the line between the multi-joint lifts Eric weights training time toward and the "small share" of single-joint work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).
133	    21	
134	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The rule is stated, not tested; the book gives no example of a decision that changed because the two totals were separated. The fundamental/additional line is drawn for weightlifting; Inference: in other sports the line has to be redrawn from that sport's own classification. Separating totals does not say how to weight them against each other.
135	    23	
136	    24	**Example** — Inference, using the 16-group scheme on PDF 446: a week with 120 lifts above 70% in snatch, clean and jerk, pulls and squats (fundamental groups 1-12) and 200 reps of lunges, good mornings and presses (additional groups 13-15) is logged as two numbers, not as 320 reps.
137	    25	
138	    26	**Related** — [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]], [[framework--volume-intensity-and-relative-intensity-calculation]], [[case-study--vorobyev-ermakov-weightlifting-load-distributions]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]]

153	    14	# High-Volume, Lower-Intensity, Full-Range Assistance Work Lets Tendons and Ligaments Keep Pace With Speed-Strength
154	    15	
155	    16	**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification presented under Medvedev (1986), the additional (developmental) exercises have a second role: "Additional exercises, executed with large amplitude in the joints have a positive effect on developing the tendons and ligaments. It is necessary to take into consideration that the mechanical strength of the tendons and ligaments increases comparatively slowly during training. The forced development of speed-strength can result in a discrepancy between the increase in the muscular speed-strength capacity and the strength of the tendons and ligaments, which can lead to injury. Therefore, it is necessary to devote time to strengthening the tendons and ligaments, which is accomplished by high volume work of lower intensity. It is desirable that the movements be executed through the maximum possible joint range and in all directions. Additional exercises meet these requirements" (PDF 446 / p.435, checked against the page image).
156	    17	
157	    18	**Why it works** — The mechanism stated on the page is a rate mismatch: muscle speed-strength can rise faster than tendon and ligament strength, and the gap is where injury happens. The remedy is volume, not intensity, across full range and all directions. The page gives no tissue data. The rate claim matches the book's earlier statement of differential tissue adaptation (see [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]).
158	    19	
159	    20	**When to apply** — When speed-strength is being pushed hard ("forced development"), for example a concentrated jump or Olympic-lift block, keep assistance work that is high in volume, lower in intensity, and full-range in several directions, rather than cutting it to save time. Eric's review: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the book's point adds a tissue reason for the same caution; a quick rise in power output is itself an abrupt change for the tendon.
160	    21	
161	    22	**When NOT to apply** — No study is cited for the injury claim or for the volume prescription; doses are not given. The 8.2 entry on connective tissue says heavy or rapidly imposed loads "can play a valuable role" too (see [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]), so this passage does not mean light work is the only route. "In all directions" is written for lifters' assistance work; Inference: it does not license loaded end-range work in a joint that is already injured.
162	    23	
163	    24	**Example** — The additional groups that fit the description: lunges with the bar on the shoulders, on the chest or between the legs, good mornings (legs straight, seated), prone back extensions, and presses behind the head with a snatch grip (groups 13-15, PDF 446 / p.435 and items 76-91, PDF 449 / p.438).
164	    25

180	    14	# Bench, Squat and Deadlift Variants Come From a Few Axes: Grip and Stance, Range, Tempo, Muscle Regime, Start Condition and Resistance Type
181	    15	
182	    16	**What it is** — After the weightlifting list the authors give "Examples of Powerlifting Exercises": 40 bench press variations, 38 squat variations and 25 deadlift variations (PDF 449-451 / p.438-440, counted on the page images), followed by 41 "Hybrid Lifting Exercises" (PDF 451-452 / p.440-441). The lists carry no commentary. Inference: read across, the variants come from a small set of axes, each changed one at a time:
183	    17	- *Grip and stance*: snatch, narrow, jerk, hands-touching, reverse, thumbless grip (bench 1-4, 13, 14); narrow, parallel or turned-out feet, heels or toes raised (squat 4-8); sumo (deadlift 11).
184	    18	- *Range*: "limited range between set points on power rack" (bench 17), part-range squats, "partial range (from hang or rack)" deadlifts, box squats at "different depths, resting or just touching" (squat 30).
185	    19	- *Tempo*: "slow down, fast up," "slow down, slow up," "fast down, fast up" (bench 7-9); "different speeds over different ranges" (deadlift 7).
186	    20	- *Muscle regime*: isometric against a fixed bar, drive to stops then isometric, eccentric only, concentric only (bench 18-19, 23-24; squat 14-15, 17; deadlift 13, 16-17, 21).
187	    21	- *Start condition*: from rest on the chest, replacing the bar on the rack each rep, continuous reps without pause, from plinths (bench 5, 21-22, 26; squat 11-12, 16).
188	    22	- *Resistance type*: machines, variable resistance machines, dumbbells, "attached chains or elastic bands," load release, isokinetic dynamometer, thick bar (bench 29-30, 32, 38, 27; squat 29, 31; deadlift 15, 19, 25).
189	    23	- *Instability and oscillation*: balance board, balls of the feet, "oscillating over small range" (squat 25-26, 37; deadlift 14; bench 39-40).
190	    24	
191	    25	**Why it works** — The book gives no rationale on these pages. Inference: each axis shifts one feature of the lift (sticking point, rate of force development, regime, stability demand) while keeping the main pattern, which is the same logic as the weightlifting list's start positions, stops and tempos.
192	    26	
193	    27	**When to apply** — When a lift stalls or a block needs variety without leaving the pattern, change one axis and keep the rest. For hybrids, the authors' note: "the clean pull and deadlift, or press, push-press and jerk, or front and back squats may be interchanged in several cases to suit one's specific needs," and "one may also use dumbbells instead of barbells for some of the exercises" (PDF 451-452 / p.440-441).
194	    28	
195	    29	**When NOT to apply** — The lists are menus with no dosing, no ranking and no evidence of effect. "Squats, standing on balance board, light to moderate load" (squat 26) appears without comment, while the authors elsewhere set a minimax test for balance tools (see [[principle--minimax-principle-of-training-economics]]). The axis grouping is this entry's, not the book's.
196	    30	
197	    31	**Example** — Squat 2, "Powerlifting Back Squat (half-squat, bar low on shoulders, feet wide, buttocks thrust back)," set against squat 1, "Weightlifting Back Squat (full squat, bar high on shoulders, torso fairly erect)" (PDF 450 / p.439, checked against the page image), changes range, bar position and stance at once, which is why the book then labels later variants "(WL or PWL)."
198	    32	
199	    33	**Related** — [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]], [[framework--hybrid-repetitions-and-hybrid-sets]], [[framework--contrast-methods-load-release-pneumatics-heavy-light-set]], [[case-study--box-squat-with-free-weights-plus-elastic-bands]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]]

201	     1	---
202	     2	type: library-entry
203	     3	kind: claim
204	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
205	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
206	     6	chapter: "8.5"
207	     7	topic: overtraining definition
208	     8	category: [overtraining, fatigue, adaptation, recovery, monitoring]
209	     9	confidence: untested
210	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
211	    11	created: 2026-10-13
212	    12	---
213	    13	
214	    14	# Overtraining Is Stress-Adaptation Imbalance Accumulated Over Time; Exhaustion Is the Short-Term Version
215	    15	
216	    16	**What it is** — The authors open 8.5: "Overtraining and exhaustion are both a consequence of imbalance between stress and adaptability of the body." Successful adaptation "implicates supercompensatory (adaptive reconstructive) processes," while unsuccessful adaptation "depletes the current adaptation reserves (see 1.14)." "Exhaustion is the systemic result of short-term imbalance, whereas overtraining is the result of imbalance accumulated over a prolonged period" (PDF 452 / p.441, checked against the page image). Because Selye's 'energy' is not only metabolic energy, "overtraining is closely related to an inadequate rate of recovery and adaptation of: the energy systems of the body (see 1.13); cell repair and growth mechanisms (see 1.11); hormonal systems (see 1.12 and 1.13.7); nervous processes (see 1.12)" (PDF 452-453 / p.441-442). The warning signs: "The insidious road to overtraining is signposted, not always clearly, by residual fatigue or soreness, persistent minor injuries, loss of motivation, or lack of progress" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image).
217	    17	
218	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: "Any imbalance causes the body's homeostatic mechanisms to decrease stress or enforce short- or long-term rest to prevent further damage" (PDF 452). They cite the Two Factor Model for "the central role played by fatigue in the overall preparedness process," and warn that "the popular practice of forcing oneself through these negative phases can lead to acute or chronic injury" (PDF 453). Inference: on this view the symptoms are the body's own brake, so pushing through them overrides the protection the authors describe.
219	    19	
220	    20	**When to apply** — When a run of the four signs appears together (residual fatigue or soreness, recurring minor injuries, falling motivation, stalled progress), treat it as accumulated imbalance, not as a single bad day. The authors require that "the existence of acute or chronic fatigue symptoms be recognised by the athlete and his coach" (PDF 453). Eric's review: "The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 33, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)). Inference: the four signs are the kind of thing a coach's eye flags; Eric's tracked measures are then where to look.
221	    21	
222	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The section is a conceptual framing with no data. The authors themselves say the road is signposted "not always clearly," so the four signs are neither sensitive nor specific. The cross-reference to the Two Factor Model is printed as "1.15.3" on PDF 453 and as "1.16.3" on PDF 455; one of them is a misprint. "Overtraining" here is used broadly; the same page notes the current split into overtraining (chronic) and overreaching (acute) (see [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]]).
223	    23	
224	    24	**Example** — The authors' own warning case: athletes who follow the "popular practice of forcing oneself through these negative phases" risk "acute or chronic injury" (PDF 453 / p.442).
225	    25	
226	    26	**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]], [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]], [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/claim--busy-motivated-athletes-overtrain-and-prevention-needs-natural-history-data]]

228	     1	---
229	     2	type: library-entry

233	     6	chapter: "8.5"

239	    12	---
240	    13	
241	    14	# Tell General From Local Overtraining, and Acute From Chronic: One Lift Up While Another Falls Points to a Local Problem
242	    15	
243	    16	**What it is** — Two cross-cutting splits. By extent: "There are two types of overtraining: general and local. *General overtraining* affects the whole body and results in stagnation of a decrease in performance [sic], whereas *local overtraining* affects a specific body part." By time course: excessive training "is also categorised into two classes: *overtraining* (chronic excessive training) and *overreaching* (acute excessive training), so that one needs to assess if the excessive training is of an acute or chronic nature" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image). Recognising the local form: "The presence of local overtraining is relatively simple to recognise, since it is often accompanied by stiffness or soreness of a particular muscle group which does not subside with alternate days of rest. Moreover, the performance of that muscle group might be static or diminished and some of the symptoms of general overtraining, such as impaired coordination, might be present. In weight training, this situation may be revealed by outstanding performance in one supplementary exercise such as the squat, but diminished performance in another exercise such as the bench press" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image).
244	    17	
245	    18	**Why it works** — The authors give the signs, not the mechanism. Inference: if one muscle group fails to recover while the rest of the body adapts, whole-body markers can look normal, so the evidence has to come from that group's own soreness and its own lifts.
246	    19	
247	    20	**When to apply** — When soreness in one muscle group persists through alternate rest days, or when one lift climbs while another drops in the same athlete, look at the load on that region before changing the whole programme. Ask first whether the excess is acute (overreaching) or chronic (overtraining), as the authors require.
248	    21	
249	    22	**When NOT to apply** — These are observational rules with no data or thresholds; "relatively simple to recognise" is the authors' judgment. A squat-up, bench-down split can also come from programme emphasis, technique change or an upper-body injury. Inference: check the programme before calling it overtraining. The general/local split and the A/B split (see [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]]) are separate axes; A and B apply to general overtraining.
250	    23	
251	    24	**Example** — The authors' own: in weight training, "outstanding performance in one supplementary exercise such as the squat, but diminished performance in another exercise such as the bench press" (PDF 454 / p.443).
252	    25	
253	    26	**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[heuristic--six-strength-training-causes-of-overtraining-injury]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]] (palpation soreness)
254	##### FILE: framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3.md
255	     1	---
256	     2	type: library-entry
257	     3	kind: framework
258	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
259	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
260	     6	chapter: "8.5"

262	     8	category: [overtraining, autonomic, endocrine, monitoring, sympathetic, parasympathetic]
263	     9	confidence: untested
264	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
265	    11	created: 2026-10-13
266	    12	---
267	    13	
268	    14	# Two Types of General Overtraining: A (Addisonic, Parasympathetic, Quiet) and B (Basedowic, Sympathetic, Obvious), Table 8.3
269	    15	
270	    16	**What it is** — The authors tie general overtraining to the endocrine system. Fig 8.3 ("Some of the physiological control systems involved with motor processes") draws the hypothalamus linked to the central nervous system ("Fast Control") and the endocrine system ("Slow Control"), both linked to the muscular system (PDF 453 / p.442, read from the figure). Since hormones are central to stress, "it is logical to associate general overtraining, a stress related phenomenon, with some disturbance of the endocrine system," and "Researchers sometimes identify at least two types of general overtraining on this basis (Israel, 1963)" (PDF 453). *A-overtraining* (Addisonic), after Addison's disease ("diminished activity of the adrenal glands"), "affects predominantly the parasympathetic pathways" and "is difficult to detect early, due to the absence of any dramatic symptoms"; stagnation or deterioration of performance may be the first clue. *B-overtraining* (Basedowic), after Basedow's disease ("thyroid hyperactivity"), "affects predominantly the sympathetic pathways" and, "as the classical type of overtraining with its abundance of symptoms, is easy to diagnose" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image). Table 8.3, "Symptomatic comparison of A and B types of overtraining" (PDF 454 / p.443, read from the page image), A then B:
271	    17	1. Blood pressure: "diastolic increase to over 100mm Hg, during and after physical stress" / "slight increase"
272	    18	2. Coordination: impaired / "impaired, with increased reaction time"
273	    19	3. Bodymass: normal / decrease
274	    20	4. Endurance: "slight increase in tiredness" / "tendency to tire easily"
275	    21	5. Sleep requirements: "no increase" / increase
276	    22	6. Resting pulse: low / elevated
277	    23	7. Body temperature: normal / "slightly increased"
278	    24	8. Appetite: normal / reduced
279	    25	9. Metabolism: normal / "altered, with increased tendency to sweat: abnormally increased breathing rate under stress"
280	    26	10. General muscle soreness: "little or none" / "mild to pronounced, with tendency to muscle stiffness and pain"
281	    27	11. General resistance: normal / "tendency to headaches, colds, fever blisters; prolonged recuperation"
282	    28	12. Recovery time: "normal or slightly increased" / increased
283	    29	13. Psychological changes: "none, other than slight loss in motivation" / "nervousness, poor motivation, inner unease, eventual depression"
284	    30	The authors add that overtraining "has also been shown to be associated with electrocardiographic changes, in particular a smaller T wave," so the table "could no doubt be extended" (PDF 454).
285	    31	
286	    32	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale is the endocrine link: the adrenals "selectively prepare the skeletal muscle for physical activity in the face of stress," thyroxine raises the rate cells burn fuel and joins "anti-stress responses" (PDF 453). Inference: the two pictures follow the autonomic direction, so B shows raised drive (pulse, temperature, sweating, nervousness) and A shows damped drive with few signs.
287	    33	
288	    34	**When to apply** — As a reminder that a quiet athlete can be overtrained. Inference: a low resting pulse with stalled performance and no complaints fits the A picture, which the authors say is "difficult to detect early"; a performance check is then the main signal.
289	    35	
290	    36	**When NOT to apply** — The table carries one citation (Israel, 1963) and no data, thresholds or sample; `untested`. The text on PDF 453 says the types "are compared in Table 8.2," but the table on PDF 454 is printed as Table 8.3; Table 8.2 is Matveyev's sport classification on PDF 445. Two library sources split overtraining the same way but differ in detail: Samuels lists low resting blood pressure for the parasympathetic type, while Table 8.3 gives an A-type diastolic rise "during and after physical stress," a different measurement condition, not the same claim. Samuels has disturbed sleep in the sympathetic type and none in the parasympathetic, and Table 8.3 has increased sleep requirement only in B; these align. Not marked `contested`. Inference: naming the types after Addison's and Basedow's diseases is an analogy; the book does not claim athletes have those diseases.
291	    37	
292	    38	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: the B type, "the classical type of overtraining with its abundance of symptoms, is easy to diagnose," while for the A type, "Suspicion that something is amiss may be aroused by the appearance of stagnation or deterioration of the athlete's performance" (PDF 453 / p.442).
293	    39	
294	    40	**Related** — [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/framework--sympathetic-and-parasympathetic-overtraining-signs]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]], [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]]

     1	---

     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning

     9	confidence: untested

    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Classify Every Exercise as Competitive, Special Preparatory or General Preparatory Before Placing It in a Phase
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The paragraph that closes 8.3 sits on PDF 444 / p.433 above the 8.4 heading, and leads straight into it. The authors say exercises "may be divided into three broad categories for most sports": *Competitive Exercises*, "exercises that are actually performed in competition"; *Special Physical Preparation exercises*, which "may be similar to the competitive movements or largely dissimilar exercises that may develop the specific motor qualities required in the sport"; and *General Physical Preparation exercises*, "usually different from the competition movements in type, pattern, mode of execution and speed, and ... intended for general development to form a foundation for later stages of training" (PDF 444 / p.433, checked against the page image). Section 8.4.1 then gives the Russian source. In Russia "not only is all training broadly divided into general preparatory, special preparatory and competitive phases, but all exercises are classified similarly," a practice the authors credit to A Novikov (1949), who held that classification is "the most important foundation for education and training" (PDF 444). They quote Matveyev, in "revised excerpts" from the English translation of *The Fundamentals of Sports Training* (1981): the key distinction is an exercise's "similarity or difference compared with the specific movements characterising a given sport," which splits exercises "into *competition* and *preparatory* exercises, then into *special preparatory* and *general preparatory* exercises." Competition exercises are "performed in the same way as during competition." Special preparatory exercises "consist of elements of the competition actions and variations of them, as well as actions similar to them, in terms of the form and the character of the abilities displayed," and divide into *preliminary exercises* "(to help the athlete master the movement)" and *developmental exercises* "(to develop physical qualities)" (Matveyev, quoted on PDF 444 / p.433).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' claim: "The ability to place all exercises (and the different techniques of using them) into these categories enables one to avoid making any serious errors in selecting any of them to achieve a specific training purpose at a given stage of a periodisation scheme" (PDF 444 / p.433). Matveyev's reason for keeping competition exercises in training: without them "it is impossible to fully equip the athlete with the specific requirements of the given sport, and stimulate the development of specific preparedness" (PDF 444). Inference: the classification works as a filter because each class has a different job, so a mismatch between the class and the phase is visible before the session is run.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When building a phase or auditing a programme, tag each exercise (and each way of using it, since the authors include "the different techniques of using them") with its class, and check that the mix fits the phase. Matveyev notes that preliminary and developmental exercises "are introduced at the different stages of training in unequal proportions" (PDF 444). Eric's review: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: Eric's four-step spectrum matches Matveyev's tree if "specific preparation" is read as the preliminary subtype and "specific development" as the developmental subtype; the book gives Matveyev's subtypes, not Bondarchuk's four classes.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The classification is presented as a Russian convention with no data on whether using it reduces selection errors; "avoid making any serious errors" is the authors' assertion. The boundary between special and general preparatory is loose in the book's own wording: a special preparatory exercise may be "largely dissimilar" to the competition movement (PDF 444), so similarity of form alone does not decide the class. The authors elsewhere warn that GPP and SPP can merge (see [[heuristic--gpp-and-spp-form-one-unit-curtail-gpp-for-advanced-athletes]]). The Matveyev text is a revised excerpt, so exact wording may be the authors' edit rather than the translation.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Inference, built from the categories: in a sprinter's programme, the sprint race is competitive; resisted sprints and starts are special preparatory, with technique drills as preliminary and sled pulls as developmental; back squats and general circuits are general preparatory. The book's own worked case is weightlifting (8.4.2, PDF 445 / p.434), where the snatch and clean and jerk are Group 1, auxiliary lifts Group 2, and general physical training Group 3 (see [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]]).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] (Bondarchuk splits the special group into specialized-preparatory and specialized-developmental classes; Matveyev keeps one special preparatory group with two subtypes. Different taxonomies, not a conflict), [[heuristic--general-preparatory-exercises-three-functions-and-two-selection-rules]], [[framework--matveyev-categorisation-of-competitive-exercises-table-8-2]], [[framework--general-and-specific-components-of-a-training-programme]], [[heuristic--dynamic-correspondence-means-matching-motor-characteristics-not-copying-the-sport-movement]], [[heuristic--gpp-and-spp-form-one-unit-curtail-gpp-for-advanced-athletes]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Choose General Preparatory Exercises for Three Jobs, Limited by Time and Equipment, and Shaped by the Sport
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the Matveyev excerpt the authors quote, general preparatory exercises are "the fundamental, practical means to achieve the athlete's general preparation." They are "much broader in scope and more varied than the other groups," and their list "is theoretically unlimited, though practically their use is restricted by the time which can be taken without detriment from other means of training and by the availability of equipment" (PDF 444 / p.433, checked against the page image). Two selection requirements: "Firstly, the athlete must have a comprehensive background of multi-faceted physical education. Secondly, the contents of the athlete's general preparation should reflect the specifics of the sport." Three functions: "(a) to form, strengthen or restore motor skills which play an auxiliary, facilitatory role in sport perfecting (b) to teach abilities developed insufficiently by the given sport, increase the general work capacity or preserve it (c) to provide active rest, promote restoration after strenuous loading and counteract the monotony of training" (PDF 445 / p.434, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Matveyev's statement is that "These functions define the role of the general preparatory exercises in the athlete's training programme" (PDF 445). Inference: each function names a gap the sport itself does not fill (auxiliary skills, neglected abilities, recovery and variety), so a general exercise earns its place by filling one of those gaps, not by being "general."
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When deciding whether a general exercise belongs in the plan, name which of (a), (b) or (c) it serves, check it against the time cost "without detriment from other means," and check that it still "reflect[s] the specifics of the sport." Function (c) matches the authors' restorative use of GPP in the concentrated-loading models (see [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]]). Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: function (c) is a load-design route to recovery, so it fits that stance without adding a recovery modality.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The list is Matveyev's classification, not a tested rule; no data are given on which functions matter most. The first requirement assumes an athlete who already has "a comprehensive background of multi-faceted physical education"; Inference: with a poorly prepared athlete the order reverses, and building that background becomes the job of the general work itself. The authors elsewhere say standard GPP should be curtailed for advanced athletes (see [[heuristic--gpp-and-spp-form-one-unit-curtail-gpp-for-advanced-athletes]]), so "theoretically unlimited" is not a licence to expand GPP.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The book's weightlifting case (8.4.2): general preparatory exercises for lifters are drawn from ten disciplines, including track and field ("Acceleration runs: 400 - 1000 meters," jumps, throws, "cross-country running 1-3 km"), gymnastics, sport games, cycling, rowing, swimming, winter sports and hiking, with gymnastics, acrobatics, mobility games, skating and middle-distance running named as appropriate for juveniles (PDF 447 / p.436, checked against the page image).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--competition-special-preparatory-and-general-preparatory-exercise-classes]], [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]], [[principle--minimax-principle-of-training-economics]] (the time-cost limit), [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]

    13	
    14	# Matveyev's Table 8.2: Competitive Exercises Grouped as Monostructural, Polystructural or Complexes
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors present Matveyev's "classification of competitive exercises" as a further illustration of "the meticulous attention to detail used in the Russian system" (PDF 445 / p.434). Table 8.2, "Categorisation of Competitive Exercises in Different Types of Sport," read from the page image, has three overall groupings:
    17	- *Monostructural Exercises (relatively stable forms)*: 1. Speed and Strength Exercises (A. Jumps; B. Throws (Shot, javelin, etc); C. Lifting weights; D. Sprint); 2. Cyclic Endurance (A. High intensity endurance events; B. Low and medium intensity endurance).
    18	- *Polystructural Exercises (variable forms)*: 1. Team Games (A. High intensity interval; B. Prolonged relatively continuous); 2. Sporting Combat (A. Non physical contact (fencing etc); B. Physical Contact (boxing, wrestling etc)).
    19	- *Complexes of Exercises*: 1. Dual and Combined Events with a stable content (A. Homogeneous Two-event & Combined events (skating 4-events, Alpine 3-events etc); B. Non-homogeneous dual and combined events (decathlon, pentathlon, ski dual etc)); 2. Dual and Combined Events with a periodically renewed content (A. Aesthetic Sports (gymnastics, diving, skating, acrobatics etc)).
    20	
    21	**Why it works** — The book gives the table without a stated rationale. Inference: the top split is by how stable the movement form is (fixed versus variable versus a set of events), and the second split is by the dominant quality or contact demand, which are the features that decide how specific the special preparatory work can be.
    22	
    23	**When to apply** — As a first sort when a coach meets an unfamiliar sport: place it in a cell, then borrow programming from neighbours in that cell. Inference: American football sits under Polystructural, Team Games, A (high intensity interval), the same cell as other field sports with repeated short efforts.
    24	
    25	**When NOT to apply** — The table carries no data and no stated purpose beyond illustration. Some cells are thin: Dual and Combined Events "with a periodically renewed content" has a single subgroup, aesthetic sports. Skating appears both in the homogeneous combined events and among aesthetic sports, so a sport can fall in more than one cell. The 6.7 classification by Farfel (acyclic, cyclic, complex) cuts the same sports differently, by movement organisation and energy supply (see [[framework--three-sport-groups-acyclic-cyclic-complex-for-programming]]); the two schemes are different lenses, not a conflict. Note the book reuses the label "Table 8.2" on PDF 453 / p.442 for the A/B overtraining comparison, which is printed as Table 8.3 on PDF 454.
    26	
    27	**Example** — The table's own placements: sprint and weightlifting are monostructural speed-strength exercises, while boxing and wrestling are polystructural combat with physical contact (PDF 445 / p.434, checked against the page image).
    28

    13	
    14	# Medvedev's Weightlifting Classification: Competition, Special Preparatory and General Groups, Recast as 12 Fundamental and 4 Additional Means
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors offer the Russian weightlifting scheme as a model that "may then be applied in any other sport" (PDF 445 / p.434). Per Medvedev (1986): "Group 1 consists of the competition exercises (in weightlifting, the Snatch and Clean & Jerk)"; "Group 2 combines the Special Preparatory exercises," subdivided into auxiliary snatch exercises, auxiliary clean and jerk exercises, and "auxiliary exercises for the legs, back, (torso), arms and shoulder girdle"; "Group 3 consists of General Preparatory exercises" (PDF 445, checked against the page image). The passage that follows, presented under Medvedev's classification, then regroups them by effect. Group 1 "combines the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means," mostly "in conformity with the technique of the classic Snatch and classic Clean & Jerk," lifted heavy "at great power," so it is "the fundamental group." Group 2 holds the "special preparatory (developmental) exercises," which "for the most part ... have a local effect," use "relatively light weights," develop "relatively small" power and "can be significantly different in technique" (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). "The fundamental exercises are divided into 12 groups and the additional exercises into 4 groups" (PDF 446 / p.435): fundamental 1-12 are classic snatch, squat snatch, power snatch, snatch pull, classic clean and jerk, squat clean, jerk, power clean, clean pull, barbell squats, good mornings and pressing; additional 13-16 are leg exercises, back exercises, arm and shoulder girdle exercises, and "The Snatch and Clean & Jerk Exercises with weights less than 60%" (PDF 446, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The stated reason for the regrouping: all exercises, "depending on their coordination structure, method of training and amount of resistance," develop physical qualities and contribute to "the perfecting of technical mastery" to different extents, so "it is appropriate to divide all of the exercises of the first and second groups into two independent parts" (PDF 445 / p.434). Inference: the split sorts exercises by the size of the training effect they carry, so that heavy, technique-matched lifting can be tracked apart from light local work.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When building a classification for a sport's own exercise pool, use the two passes the book models: first by resemblance (competition, special, general), then by effect (fundamental versus additional). Inference: the clean, jerk and squat variants Eric names as core work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104) would sit in the fundamental group; single-joint assistance work would be additional.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is weightlifting-specific and the book reports no outcome data for it. The source is internally loose: Group 1 is first "the competition exercises" and then "the competition and special preparatory (auxiliary) means" (PDF 445), and the light snatch and clean and jerk under 60% move to the additional group. The numbered list of "One hundred different weightlifting exercises" that follows (PDF 447-449 / p.436-438) uses its own group numbering, which jumps from Group 7 to Group 9 with no Group 8 heading (PDF 448 / p.437), and has no entry for the under-60% group. The 100-exercise list itself is not atomized here.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Pull variants show how one fundamental group expands in the 100-exercise list: snatch pulls from the floor, from below, at and above the knee, from a block, "with four, 3-second stops (at the instant of starting lift, at knees, above the knees, heels raised)," slow then fast, and combined with the full snatch (items 15-28, PDF 447-448 / p.436-437, checked against the page images).
    25

    13	
    14	# Count Fundamental and Additional Training Loads Separately, Not as One Total
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification the book presents under Medvedev (1986): "in order to more objectively assess the training influence, the athlete is subjected to exercises from Group 1, their loading is counted as fundamental, while the loading in the Group 2 is considered additional. Finally, it is important that *fundamental and additional training loads should be calculated and analysed separately*" (PDF 446 / p.435, italics in the original, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The passage's reasoning: Group 1 lifts are heavy, close to competition technique and done "at great power," while Group 2 lifts are light, local and develop "relatively small" power (PDF 445-446 / p.434-435). Inference: one tonnage total would let a large volume of light local work mask a drop in heavy competition-pattern work, or the reverse, so the two need separate columns to show what the athlete actually did.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — In any training log that sums volume (lifts, tonnage, reps above a percentage), keep at least two totals: the core lifts that carry the main training effect, and the assistance work. Inference: in a team setting this is the line between the multi-joint lifts Eric weights training time toward and the "small share" of single-joint work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The rule is stated, not tested; the book gives no example of a decision that changed because the two totals were separated. The fundamental/additional line is drawn for weightlifting; Inference: in other sports the line has to be redrawn from that sport's own classification. Separating totals does not say how to weight them against each other.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Inference, using the 16-group scheme on PDF 446: a week with 120 lifts above 70% in snatch, clean and jerk, pulls and squats (fundamental groups 1-12) and 200 reps of lunges, good mornings and presses (additional groups 13-15) is logged as two numbers, not as 320 reps.
    25

    13	
    14	# High-Volume, Lower-Intensity, Full-Range Assistance Work Lets Tendons and Ligaments Keep Pace With Speed-Strength
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the weightlifting classification presented under Medvedev (1986), the additional (developmental) exercises have a second role: "Additional exercises, executed with large amplitude in the joints have a positive effect on developing the tendons and ligaments. It is necessary to take into consideration that the mechanical strength of the tendons and ligaments increases comparatively slowly during training. The forced development of speed-strength can result in a discrepancy between the increase in the muscular speed-strength capacity and the strength of the tendons and ligaments, which can lead to injury. Therefore, it is necessary to devote time to strengthening the tendons and ligaments, which is accomplished by high volume work of lower intensity. It is desirable that the movements be executed through the maximum possible joint range and in all directions. Additional exercises meet these requirements" (PDF 446 / p.435, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The mechanism stated on the page is a rate mismatch: muscle speed-strength can rise faster than tendon and ligament strength, and the gap is where injury happens. The remedy is volume, not intensity, across full range and all directions. The page gives no tissue data. The rate claim matches the book's earlier statement of differential tissue adaptation (see [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When speed-strength is being pushed hard ("forced development"), for example a concentrated jump or Olympic-lift block, keep assistance work that is high in volume, lower in intensity, and full-range in several directions, rather than cutting it to save time. Eric's review: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the book's point adds a tissue reason for the same caution; a quick rise in power output is itself an abrupt change for the tendon.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — No study is cited for the injury claim or for the volume prescription; doses are not given. The 8.2 entry on connective tissue says heavy or rapidly imposed loads "can play a valuable role" too (see [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]), so this passage does not mean light work is the only route. "In all directions" is written for lifters' assistance work; Inference: it does not license loaded end-range work in a joint that is already injured.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The additional groups that fit the description: lunges with the bar on the shoulders, on the chest or between the legs, good mornings (legs straight, seated), prone back extensions, and presses behind the head with a snatch grip (groups 13-15, PDF 446 / p.435 and items 76-91, PDF 449 / p.438).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]], [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[framework--medvedev-weightlifting-exercise-groups-fundamental-and-additional-means]]

    14	# Bench, Squat and Deadlift Variants Come From a Few Axes: Grip and Stance, Range, Tempo, Muscle Regime, Start Condition and Resistance Type
    15	
    16	**What it is** — After the weightlifting list the authors give "Examples of Powerlifting Exercises": 40 bench press variations, 38 squat variations and 25 deadlift variations (PDF 449-451 / p.438-440, counted on the page images), followed by 41 "Hybrid Lifting Exercises" (PDF 451-452 / p.440-441). The lists carry no commentary. Inference: read across, the variants come from a small set of axes, each changed one at a time:
    17	- *Grip and stance*: snatch, narrow, jerk, hands-touching, reverse, thumbless grip (bench 1-4, 13, 14); narrow, parallel or turned-out feet, heels or toes raised (squat 4-8); sumo (deadlift 11).
    18	- *Range*: "limited range between set points on power rack" (bench 17), part-range squats, "partial range (from hang or rack)" deadlifts, box squats at "different depths, resting or just touching" (squat 30).
    19	- *Tempo*: "slow down, fast up," "slow down, slow up," "fast down, fast up" (bench 7-9); "different speeds over different ranges" (deadlift 7).
    20	- *Muscle regime*: isometric against a fixed bar, drive to stops then isometric, eccentric only, concentric only (bench 18-19, 23-24; squat 14-15, 17; deadlift 13, 16-17, 21).
    21	- *Start condition*: from rest on the chest, replacing the bar on the rack each rep, continuous reps without pause, from plinths (bench 5, 21-22, 26; squat 11-12, 16).
    22	- *Resistance type*: machines, variable resistance machines, dumbbells, "attached chains or elastic bands," load release, isokinetic dynamometer, thick bar (bench 29-30, 32, 38, 27; squat 29, 31; deadlift 15, 19, 25).
    23	- *Instability and oscillation*: balance board, balls of the feet, "oscillating over small range" (squat 25-26, 37; deadlift 14; bench 39-40).
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The book gives no rationale on these pages. Inference: each axis shifts one feature of the lift (sticking point, rate of force development, regime, stability demand) while keeping the main pattern, which is the same logic as the weightlifting list's start positions, stops and tempos.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — When a lift stalls or a block needs variety without leaving the pattern, change one axis and keep the rest. For hybrids, the authors' note: "the clean pull and deadlift, or press, push-press and jerk, or front and back squats may be interchanged in several cases to suit one's specific needs," and "one may also use dumbbells instead of barbells for some of the exercises" (PDF 451-452 / p.440-441).
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — The lists are menus with no dosing, no ranking and no evidence of effect. "Squats, standing on balance board, light to moderate load" (squat 26) appears without comment, while the authors elsewhere set a minimax test for balance tools (see [[principle--minimax-principle-of-training-economics]]). The axis grouping is this entry's, not the book's.
    30	
    31	**Example** — Squat 2, "Powerlifting Back Squat (half-squat, bar low on shoulders, feet wide, buttocks thrust back)," set against squat 1, "Weightlifting Back Squat (full squat, bar high on shoulders, torso fairly erect)" (PDF 450 / p.439, checked against the page image), changes range, bar position and stance at once, which is why the book then labels later variants "(WL or PWL)."
    32

    13	
    14	# Overtraining Is Stress-Adaptation Imbalance Accumulated Over Time; Exhaustion Is the Short-Term Version
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors open 8.5: "Overtraining and exhaustion are both a consequence of imbalance between stress and adaptability of the body." Successful adaptation "implicates supercompensatory (adaptive reconstructive) processes," while unsuccessful adaptation "depletes the current adaptation reserves (see 1.14)." "Exhaustion is the systemic result of short-term imbalance, whereas overtraining is the result of imbalance accumulated over a prolonged period" (PDF 452 / p.441, checked against the page image). Because Selye's 'energy' is not only metabolic energy, "overtraining is closely related to an inadequate rate of recovery and adaptation of: the energy systems of the body (see 1.13); cell repair and growth mechanisms (see 1.11); hormonal systems (see 1.12 and 1.13.7); nervous processes (see 1.12)" (PDF 452-453 / p.441-442). The warning signs: "The insidious road to overtraining is signposted, not always clearly, by residual fatigue or soreness, persistent minor injuries, loss of motivation, or lack of progress" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: "Any imbalance causes the body's homeostatic mechanisms to decrease stress or enforce short- or long-term rest to prevent further damage" (PDF 452). They cite the Two Factor Model for "the central role played by fatigue in the overall preparedness process," and warn that "the popular practice of forcing oneself through these negative phases can lead to acute or chronic injury" (PDF 453). Inference: on this view the symptoms are the body's own brake, so pushing through them overrides the protection the authors describe.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a run of the four signs appears together (residual fatigue or soreness, recurring minor injuries, falling motivation, stalled progress), treat it as accumulated imbalance, not as a single bad day. The authors require that "the existence of acute or chronic fatigue symptoms be recognised by the athlete and his coach" (PDF 453). Eric's review: "The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 33, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)). Inference: the four signs are the kind of thing a coach's eye flags; Eric's tracked measures are then where to look.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The section is a conceptual framing with no data. The authors themselves say the road is signposted "not always clearly," so the four signs are neither sensitive nor specific. The cross-reference to the Two Factor Model is printed as "1.15.3" on PDF 453 and as "1.16.3" on PDF 455; one of them is a misprint. "Overtraining" here is used broadly; the same page notes the current split into overtraining (chronic) and overreaching (acute) (see [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own warning case: athletes who follow the "popular practice of forcing oneself through these negative phases" risk "acute or chronic injury" (PDF 453 / p.442).
    25
