    13	
    14	# Tell General From Local Overtraining, and Acute From Chronic: One Lift Up While Another Falls Points to a Local Problem
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two cross-cutting splits. By extent: "There are two types of overtraining: general and local. *General overtraining* affects the whole body and results in stagnation of a decrease in performance [sic], whereas *local overtraining* affects a specific body part." By time course: excessive training "is also categorised into two classes: *overtraining* (chronic excessive training) and *overreaching* (acute excessive training), so that one needs to assess if the excessive training is of an acute or chronic nature" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image). Recognising the local form: "The presence of local overtraining is relatively simple to recognise, since it is often accompanied by stiffness or soreness of a particular muscle group which does not subside with alternate days of rest. Moreover, the performance of that muscle group might be static or diminished and some of the symptoms of general overtraining, such as impaired coordination, might be present. In weight training, this situation may be revealed by outstanding performance in one supplementary exercise such as the squat, but diminished performance in another exercise such as the bench press" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors give the signs, not the mechanism. Inference: if one muscle group fails to recover while the rest of the body adapts, whole-body markers can look normal, so the evidence has to come from that group's own soreness and its own lifts.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When soreness in one muscle group persists through alternate rest days, or when one lift climbs while another drops in the same athlete, look at the load on that region before changing the whole programme. Ask first whether the excess is acute (overreaching) or chronic (overtraining), as the authors require.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — These are observational rules with no data or thresholds; "relatively simple to recognise" is the authors' judgment. A squat-up, bench-down split can also come from programme emphasis, technique change or an upper-body injury. Inference: check the programme before calling it overtraining. The general/local split and the A/B split (see [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]]) are separate axes; A and B apply to general overtraining.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own: in weight training, "outstanding performance in one supplementary exercise such as the squat, but diminished performance in another exercise such as the bench press" (PDF 454 / p.443).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[heuristic--six-strength-training-causes-of-overtraining-injury]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]] (palpation soreness)

    13	
    14	# Two Types of General Overtraining: A (Addisonic, Parasympathetic, Quiet) and B (Basedowic, Sympathetic, Obvious), Table 8.3
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors tie general overtraining to the endocrine system. Fig 8.3 ("Some of the physiological control systems involved with motor processes") draws the hypothalamus linked to the central nervous system ("Fast Control") and the endocrine system ("Slow Control"), both linked to the muscular system (PDF 453 / p.442, read from the figure). Since hormones are central to stress, "it is logical to associate general overtraining, a stress related phenomenon, with some disturbance of the endocrine system," and "Researchers sometimes identify at least two types of general overtraining on this basis (Israel, 1963)" (PDF 453). *A-overtraining* (Addisonic), after Addison's disease ("diminished activity of the adrenal glands"), "affects predominantly the parasympathetic pathways" and "is difficult to detect early, due to the absence of any dramatic symptoms"; stagnation or deterioration of performance may be the first clue. *B-overtraining* (Basedowic), after Basedow's disease ("thyroid hyperactivity"), "affects predominantly the sympathetic pathways" and, "as the classical type of overtraining with its abundance of symptoms, is easy to diagnose" (PDF 453 / p.442, checked against the page image). Table 8.3, "Symptomatic comparison of A and B types of overtraining" (PDF 454 / p.443, read from the page image), A then B:
    17	1. Blood pressure: "diastolic increase to over 100mm Hg, during and after physical stress" / "slight increase"
    18	2. Coordination: impaired / "impaired, with increased reaction time"
    19	3. Bodymass: normal / decrease
    20	4. Endurance: "slight increase in tiredness" / "tendency to tire easily"
    21	5. Sleep requirements: "no increase" / increase
    22	6. Resting pulse: low / elevated
    23	7. Body temperature: normal / "slightly increased"
    24	8. Appetite: normal / reduced
    25	9. Metabolism: normal / "altered, with increased tendency to sweat: abnormally increased breathing rate under stress"
    26	10. General muscle soreness: "little or none" / "mild to pronounced, with tendency to muscle stiffness and pain"
    27	11. General resistance: normal / "tendency to headaches, colds, fever blisters; prolonged recuperation"
    28	12. Recovery time: "normal or slightly increased" / increased
    29	13. Psychological changes: "none, other than slight loss in motivation" / "nervousness, poor motivation, inner unease, eventual depression"
    30	The authors add that overtraining "has also been shown to be associated with electrocardiographic changes, in particular a smaller T wave," so the table "could no doubt be extended" (PDF 454).
    31	
    32	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale is the endocrine link: the adrenals "selectively prepare the skeletal muscle for physical activity in the face of stress," thyroxine raises the rate cells burn fuel and joins "anti-stress responses" (PDF 453). Inference: the two pictures follow the autonomic direction, so B shows raised drive (pulse, temperature, sweating, nervousness) and A shows damped drive with few signs.
    33	
    34	**When to apply** — As a reminder that a quiet athlete can be overtrained. Inference: a low resting pulse with stalled performance and no complaints fits the A picture, which the authors say is "difficult to detect early"; a performance check is then the main signal.
    35	
    36	**When NOT to apply** — The table carries one citation (Israel, 1963) and no data, thresholds or sample; `untested`. The text on PDF 453 says the types "are compared in Table 8.2," but the table on PDF 454 is printed as Table 8.3; Table 8.2 is Matveyev's sport classification on PDF 445. Two library sources split overtraining the same way but differ in detail: Samuels lists low resting blood pressure for the parasympathetic type, while Table 8.3 gives an A-type diastolic rise "during and after physical stress," a different measurement condition, not the same claim. Samuels has disturbed sleep in the sympathetic type and none in the parasympathetic, and Table 8.3 has increased sleep requirement only in B; these align. Not marked `contested`. Inference: naming the types after Addison's and Basedow's diseases is an analogy; the book does not claim athletes have those diseases.
    37	
    38	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: the B type, "the classical type of overtraining with its abundance of symptoms, is easy to diagnose," while for the A type, "Suspicion that something is amiss may be aroused by the appearance of stagnation or deterioration of the athlete's performance" (PDF 453 / p.442).
    39	
    40	**Related** — [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/framework--sympathetic-and-parasympathetic-overtraining-signs]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]], [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]]

308	    13	
309	    14	# Six Strength-Training Causes of Overtraining Injury to Check First
310	    15	
311	    16	**What it is** — The authors' list: "In the case of strength training, overtraining injuries may be the result of too many repetitions or sets, regular training with near maximum loads, training the same muscle groups too frequently, inadequate recovery periods, insufficient rest or faulty execution of any movement" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image). Six causes: (1) too many repetitions or sets; (2) regular training with near-maximum loads; (3) training the same muscle groups too frequently; (4) inadequate recovery periods; (5) insufficient rest; (6) faulty execution of any movement.
312	    17	
313	    18	**Why it works** — The page gives the list without a mechanism. Inference: causes 1-5 are dose (volume, intensity, frequency, and recovery between and outside sessions) and cause 6 is technique, so the list splits a strength-room injury into "too much" versus "done wrong," which point to different fixes.
314	    19	
315	    20	**When to apply** — As an audit sequence when a lifter develops an overuse complaint or a local overtraining picture (see [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]]): check sets and reps, the share of near-maximal work, how often the same group is hit, rest between sessions, rest outside training, and technique. Eric's review: "Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 109, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: that maxim addresses causes 2 and 6 directly.
316	    21	
317	    22	**When NOT to apply** — No data, no thresholds and no ranking among the six; the list says what "may" cause injury. "Inadequate recovery periods" and "insufficient rest" overlap and the book does not separate them. The 8.2 discussion splits overtraining injuries into "overload injuries (caused by too large a load at any instant) and overuse injuries (caused by very frequent application of a given load)" (PDF 438 / p.427; see [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]]). Inference: cause 2 maps mainly to overload and causes 1 and 3 to overuse; the 8.5 list does not make that mapping itself.
318	    23	
319	    24	**Example** — Inference, applied: a lifter benching heavy four days a week who reports shoulder soreness that persists through rest days shows causes 2 and 3 at once; cutting near-maximal sessions to one and the bench frequency to two is the first test, before any treatment.
320	    25	
321	    26	**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]], [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]]

336	    14	# Find the Optimum Stress Level Rather Than Avoiding Stress; Planned, Manageable Doses Build Tolerance
337	    15	
338	    16	**What it is** — Closing the overtraining discussion, the authors quote Selye: "The goal is certainly not to avoid stress - stress is a part of life. It is a natural by-product of all our activities .... But in order to express yourself fully, you must first find your optimum stress level and then use your adaptation energy at a rate and in a direction adjusted to the innate structure of your mind and body. It is not easy .... It takes much practice and almost constant self-analysis" (Selye, 1956). They read it as a definition of a programme: "a carefully designed sequence of physical and mental stresses in given conditioning workouts, with one's condition being constantly monitored and restoration being planned in a way and at a rate appropriate to one's current level of stress" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image). The same idea returns at the end of 8.6: "*Superadaptation* (supercompensation) or *innoculation* against specific stresses is possible by exposing yourself to properly structured doses of manageable stress," and "Very significantly, stress avoidance can make you more vulnerable to future stresses" (PDF 467 / p.456, checked against the page image).
339	    17	
340	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning on PDF 467: "The existence of supercompensatory processes implies that planned exposure to manageable stresses may enable one to cope with higher levels of stress" (item 12), and "Regular exposure to a stressor may produce either adaptation or sensitisation, so that the same level of stress may not produce the same response at a later stage" (item 10). Inference: avoidance gives no adaptation signal, so tolerance does not rise; too much gives sensitisation instead of adaptation; the target is the dose between.
341	    19	
342	    20	**When to apply** — When deciding how much to protect an athlete from load. Eric's review: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 40, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: Eric's "culture of fear" point and the authors' "stress avoidance can make you more vulnerable" make the same argument against under-loading. The authors' own requirement is the second half of the sentence: condition "constantly monitored" and restoration planned to the current stress.
343	    21	
344	    22	**When NOT to apply** — Selye's quote is a general life principle from 1956, not a training study; the authors offer no data that stress avoidance raises vulnerability in athletes. "Optimum" is not defined; item 9 on PDF 467 itself says "The concept of stress optimisation is not always accurate." The principle does not license loading through the warning signs in 8.5 (see [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]]).
345	    23	
346	    24	**Example** — The authors' own definition of an effective programme, quoted above, ends with restoration "planned in a way and at a rate appropriate to one's current level of stress" (PDF 454 / p.443): load and restoration are dosed together, not one after the other.
347	    25	
348	    26	**Related** — [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]], [[principle--prepare-athletes-for-risky-movements-instead-of-avoiding-them]], [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]

361	    12	---
362	    13	
363	    14	# Restoration Is Planned Into Training and Is Not Rehabilitation; Most Rehabilitation Follows Failed Pedagogical Restoration
364	    15	
365	    16	**What it is** — The authors open 8.6: "Restoration is an integral part of overall training and practice, so that it must be applied with the short-term and long-term goals constantly in mind. A comprehensive training programme alternates different training techniques with situationally appropriate restorative means." The distinction: "*restoration* in training and competition is not synonymous with *rehabilitation*, which refers to the treatment of overtraining, illness or injury" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). They return to it on the next page: "Restoration is an integral part of the overall training programme, planned to fit in at the most effective and appropriate stages of training. Rehabilitation refers to therapy to restore an injured athlete to full functional capability. Very often the need for rehabilitation is the consequence of inadequate restoration, especially imperfect pedagogical restoration, i.e. a training schedule which produces overtraining" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image).
366	    17	
367	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' causal claim is in the last sentence: a schedule that overtrains creates the injuries that then need rehabilitation. "Although accidents can happen which are largely outside the control of the athlete, the essence of training is to maximise performance and minimise injuries, pain and soreness" (PDF 456). Inference: on this view, restoration is a planning job owned by whoever writes the training, while rehabilitation is a treatment job, so a rise in rehab caseload is first a question about the programme.
368	    19	
369	    20	**When to apply** — When rehab cases cluster, audit the training schedule ("pedagogical restoration") before adding treatments. When planning, put restoration in the plan at set stages rather than leaving it to the athlete's request. Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Eric's load-design approach is what the authors call pedagogical restoration; the book's other two classes (medico-biological and psychological, see [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]]) have no counterpart in the baseline.
370	    21	
371	    22	**When NOT to apply** — "Very often" is not quantified and no injury data are given. Accidents fall outside the claim by the authors' own words.

390	    14	# Rotate Restorative Means: The Same Form at Most Once or Twice a Week, and a Day Off After Two Days of a Local Procedure
391	    15	
392	    16	**What it is** — The authors report the Russian dosing rule: "With prolonged use of any given means of restoration, the recuperative effect decreases, so that Russian experts usually recommend that the same restorative means should not be applied more than once or twice a week in the same form. They consider that, in applying local-effect procedures, it is advisable to have a single day's break after every two days of application. In particular, the body adapts more rapidly to local-effect restorative means than to general restorative means (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). They add that no single modality is enough: "Massage is not enough, saunas are part of the picture, reflexology is limited; all individual modalities are insufficient to guarantee optimal restoration in modern sport" (PDF 455). Later they restate it as "a recurrent theme throughout this book, namely that overuse of any technique leads to eventual ineffectiveness," and cite "a *complementarity effect* produced by the integrated use of several restorative means and methods carefully introduced at specific stages of a training programme" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image).
393	    17	
394	    18	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is habituation: the body adapts to a repeated restorative stimulus, faster to local than to general means, so its effect fades (PDF 455). Inference: this is the same accommodation logic the book applies to training means, where a means loses effect with repeated use and must be replaced.
395	    19	
396	    20	**When to apply** — When a team uses one recovery modality daily (the same massage, the same contrast bath, the same compression device), rotate forms through the week, and after two consecutive days of a local procedure on the same area, skip a day. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the rotation rule gives a dosing limit for the technology Eric already treats as secondary.
397	    21	
398	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The rule is cited to Siff & Yessis (1992) with no study data on these pages; the numbers (once or twice a week, one day off after two) are expert recommendations. "In the same form" leaves open how different two forms must be to count as different. Inference: the habituation claim concerns restorative effect, not safety; it is not a reason to stop a medically prescribed treatment.
399	    23	
400	    24	**Example** — The Soviet track cycling programme applied the rule across the year: "Because the same restorative means diminish their effectiveness when they are used over prolonged periods, the restorative means were alternated, regarding both content and volume, depending on the stage of the annual cycle" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image; see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]).
401	    25	
402	    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]]

417	    14	# Train on Incomplete Restoration Only for 2-3 Days, in a Healthy Athlete, With Full Restoration and Medical Cover After
418	    15	
419	    16	**What it is** — The authors: "It may also be inappropriate to routinely apply restoration on a frequent basis, since increase in work capacity can be stimulated by using workouts which are specially calculated to produce incomplete restoration." This is done by "prescribing some individual sessions which are especially demanding for some body zones or processes or the use of several sessions per day for a limited period" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image; the scan's right margin is cut on this page and the words "capacity" and "processes" are partly reconstructed). The authors cite Kopysov (1980) for the recommendation of "Some authorities" that in the period immediately before competitions, "especially in the strength and power sports," it is often advisable to run intense workouts with minimal restoration "unless there are very clear indications" that it is needed (PDF 461, paraphrased across clipped words). Zalessky's (1980) rules for "all *incomplete restoration* workouts": "The athlete should be completely healthy and in good functional state"; "Incomplete restoration should not last for more than 2-3 days"; "After such workout phases, all means should be used to facilitate full restoration"; "Medical guidance or assistance should always be available during such phases" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).
420	    17	
421	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that work capacity can be stimulated by planned under-recovery (PDF 461), echoing the 8.6 opening that "Full restoration can sometimes be undesirable" (PDF 455 / p.444). Inference: the four rules bound the risk of that stimulus, so a short overreach is followed by a full rebound instead of sliding into the accumulated imbalance the book calls overtraining.
422	    19	
423	    20	**When to apply** — When planning a deliberate overreach (a shock microcycle, several sessions per day for a short block, or a pre-competition phase in a strength or power sport), check all four of Zalessky's conditions and schedule the full-restoration phase before the block starts.
424	    21	
425	    22	**When NOT to apply** — Not in an athlete who is ill, injured or already showing overtraining signs (the first rule). Not for longer than 2-3 days. Not without access to medical help; Inference: in a college setting that means Athletic Medicine is told before the block. Kopysov's minimal-restoration advice is stated for "the strength and power sports"; the book does not extend it to team sports. No study data are given for any of the rules.
426	    23	
427	    24	**Example** — The authors' two ways of creating incomplete restoration: sessions "especially demanding for some body zones" or "several sessions per day for a limited period" (PDF 461 / p.450). Inference: a two-day block of twice-daily lower-body sessions before a deload week fits both the method and the 2-3 day limit.
428	    25

444	    14	# Three Classes of Restoration: Pedagogical (Coaching), Medico-Biological and Psychological, Plus Natural Recovery Outside Training
445	    15	
446	    16	**What it is** — "The Russians usually recognise three classes of restoration (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image):
447	    17	- *Pedagogical (coaching) restoration* "employs carefully periodised programmes to optimise the balance between training stresses and natural recuperative processes." It includes "combinational training, known in the West as 'cross training'," active rest, and "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities" after "demanding strength training sessions." Micro-, meso- and macrocycles, with the preparatory period split into General and Special Physical Preparation, exist "specifically to promote supercompensation via suitable phasing of loading and restoration regimes (see Ch 6)."
448	    18	- *Medico-biological restoration* covers "therapeutic measures offered by medical and allied practitioners," sometimes split into physiotherapeutic and pharmacological measures. Physical measures divide into natural means ("massage, showers, heat, sunlight and training outdoors") and additional means ("electrostimulation, electrosleep, diathermy, acupuncture, baro-chambers, laser therapy and ultrasound").
449	    19	- *Psychological restoration* "involves management of the mental state": hypnosis, self-hypnosis, auto-suggestion, autogenics, visualisation, progressive relaxation, guided imagery, music therapy and learning techniques, some using biofeedback or electrodermal devices.
450	    20	Beyond these, "it is essential to encourage natural recovery relating to family, living conditions, lifestyle, nutrition, leisure activities, beneficial socialisation, team atmosphere, work conditions, spiritual needs and coaching team interaction" (PDF 456). A later restatement (PDF 458 / p.447, read from the page image) puts pedagogical methods "outside the scope of this text" and splits the rest into physical, medical and psychological means. Table 8.5 subdivides them: physical (passive, active, combined); medical (pharmacological, psychiatric, surgical, nutritional, combined); psychological (therapist-administered, self-administered, combined). Table 8.6 lists physical means in three columns, active means mainly in the last (for example physical activity, recreational sport, manual labour, dance, play, postural realignment, breathing regimens, progressive relaxation, Tai Chi, yoga); Table 8.7 lists 14 psychological means from psychotherapy to "Laughter/tears" (PDF 459 / p.448).
451	    21	
452	    22	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the system is its specificity: "The Russian restoration system recognises the *specificity of each technique or sequence of techniques* for a particular sport, phase of training, individual athlete, time of the day, type of stress and type of fitness," applied "before, during, shortly after and a long time after training and competitions," with "Meticulous records" of daily physical and psychological state (PDF 456). On natural recovery: "problems which lie outside the training setting can easily predominate over training problems in determining the success of the athlete in competition" (PDF 456).
453	    23	
454	    24	**When to apply** — As a coverage check on a recovery plan: is there a pedagogical element (load phasing, active rest), a medico-biological element (by whom), a psychological element, and attention to life outside training? The authors also note that "the athlete is encouraged to shed dependence on the therapist and to learn *self-restoration* procedures (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456). Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: by the book's scheme that is the pedagogical class only.
455	    25	
456	    26	**When NOT to apply** — The categories are descriptive; the authors say Table 8.5 "should not be regarded as definitive or exclusive" (PDF 458). The lists mix well-studied means with ones that have little support (for example "Religion," "Screaming/shouting" in Table 8.7; "Therapeutic Touch," "Aromatherapy" in Table 8.6); inclusion is not endorsement of effect. Inference: the medico-biological class includes pharmacological means; anything in that class sits with the medical staff, not the strength coach.
457	    27	
458	    28	**Example** — The pedagogical example the authors give: "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities can also be very useful for promoting recovery after demanding strength training sessions" (PDF 456 / p.445).
459	    29

475	    14	# Belief and Rapport Carry Much of a Restoration Technique's Effect, Which Is Both a Tool and a Confound
476	    15	
477	    16	**What it is** — The authors: "Certainly, many of these techniques may work because they are placebos, because the user believes in them. Yet, this is a very good reason not to dismiss them." If the mind can be focused "by an apparently illogical or foolish concept to perform unusual feats of performance or healing, then it is vital that we uncover the underlying physiological principles which make the *placebo effect* (or 'faith factor') so powerful. Placebos can produce positive and negative effects; it is up to science to sift the useful from the harmful" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). The same effect "can also confound the validity of many restoration techniques, which work not because of any special merits, but because the practitioner persuades the user of its value." Hence "Virtually every claim by one massage therapist will be countered by another 'expert'" (PDF 455). On rapport: "the therapy often succeeds because of the rapport between therapist and client," and in sports restoration "*The rapport between you and the athlete is central to the success of the therapy*. In short, the belief of the athlete in you and your therapy (and sometimes an outside force, depending on the athlete's belief system) is an integral part of successful restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445, italics in the original, checked against the page image).
478	    17	
479	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "physical and mental healing are inextricably linked," so "one cannot separate the therapy from the therapist" (PDF 456). They draw the research consequence: "great care has to be taken to choose experimental and control groups and to exclude as far as possible all confounding factors such as the placebo effect and human interaction" (PDF 456). The 8.6 closing list makes the same point as propositions: "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it," and a technique "obtained at high cost," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or that "appeals to the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user is more likely to succeed" (items 1-4, PDF 467 / p.456).
480	    19	
481	    20	**When to apply** — Two uses. Practice: before using any restoration means, "consider the background and attitudes of the athlete, because these factors can have a profound effect on the efficacy of any regime" (PDF 458 / p.447). Evaluation: when a staff member reports that a modality works, ask whether the comparison controlled for belief and attention. Inference: Eric's account of abandoned wellness surveys, where athletes learned what answers the survey rewarded (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89), is a reminder that self-report after a treatment carries the same bias.
482	    21	
483	    22	**When NOT to apply** — These are the authors' opinions; no placebo-controlled data are given here. Two pages later the authors push the other way: "This [sic] is sometimes a tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," which their Russian research summary is meant "to correct" (PDF 465 / p.454; see [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]]). The two positions are not a contradiction in the book's own terms: belief adds to some real effects, and confounds the rest. Using belief deliberately raises an honesty question the book does not address.
484	    23	
485	    24	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: "one therapist will swear that aromatherapy with a certain fragrance will help, while another may claim the opposite. Another will extol the virtue of deep transverse friction for adhesions, whereas yet another will have equal success with therapeutic touch" (PDF 455 / p.444).
486	    25	
487	    26	**Related** — [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]]

502	    14	# Prescribe Restoration Like a Drug: Ten Prescription Features, Twelve Stress Factors, Eight P-Factors, Five Questions, Then Means Before Methods
503	    15	
504	    16	**What it is** — Under "Application of Restoration Measures" the authors set a four-step checklist (PDF 457 / p.446, checked against the page image):
505	    17	1. Features of therapeutic prescription to understand first: indications; contraindications; effects; side-effects; dosage; directions for use; special precautions; symptoms of misuse; treatment of misuse; dependence on therapy.
506	    18	2. Effects to analyse on the person under stress: perception of the stress and its effects; attitude towards the stress; sensory input associated with it; motor activity and its effect on it; response of body and mind; "Hierarchies of stresses acting at any instant"; intensity or quality; volume or quantity; density or concentration; duration; onset; causes.
507	    19	3. Factors to examine "before undertaking any form of therapy": procedures (types of therapy); purpose of therapy; person; practitioner; place; period; position; pain/pleasure.
508	    20	4. Questions: "Is it - Appropriate, Effective, Sufficient, Safe, Enjoyable?"
509	    21	Then: "Once you have applied this checklist, you may now select the appropriate restoration means and methods for a given person at a given time." The two terms differ: "The *means* refers to the broad general type of restoration measure (e.g. massage), whereas the *method* refers to that specific technique chosen (e.g. kneading massage) which falls within that means" (PDF 457 / p.446).
510	    22	
511	    23	**Why it works** — The authors' premise: restoration techniques, "like any other therapies," must be prescribed with an understanding of these features (PDF 457). Inference: listing misuse, dependence and side-effects alongside effects treats a recovery modality as a dose with a cost, which is the point the book makes elsewhere about routine restoration blunting adaptation.
512	    24	
513	    25	**When to apply** — Before adding any recovery modality to a team routine, or when an athlete asks for one. The checklist parallels the authors' P-factor checklist for exercise prescription in 8.3 (see [[framework--exercise-checklist-and-nine-p-factors-of-exercise-prescription]]). Inference: "Dependence on therapy" is the item most often skipped in practice, and it links to the authors' aim that athletes learn self-restoration.
514	    26	
515	    27	**When NOT to apply** — The checklist is a list of headings without criteria; it tells the practitioner what to consider, not what to decide. It gives no order of priority among the 35 items. Inference: in a team setting, steps 2 and 3 are only practical for individual cases, not for roster-wide routines. The means/methods distinction is terminological; it does not imply that methods within a means are interchangeable.
516	    28	
517	    29	**Example** — The authors' own: massage is a *means*; kneading massage is a *method* within it (PDF 457 / p.446). Table 8.8 then lists 20 massage methods within that one means (PDF 459 / p.448; see [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]]).

534	    14	# What Stress Changes (Table 8.4), and Why Motor Control Belongs on the Monitoring List
535	    15	
536	    16	**What it is** — Table 8.4, "Functions affected by physiological and psychological stress," introduced as "some of the symptoms of overtraining stress" (PDF 456 / p.445), lists 20 functions in three columns (PDF 457 / p.446, read from the page image): heart rate; blood pressure; muscular tension; muscle irritability; pain threshold; brain rhythms; breathing patterns; sleep patterns; body temperature; concentration and alertness; digestion, gastric acidity; endocrine secretion; immune response; fine motor control; reaction time; posture; pupil size (of the eye); general irritability, mood, stability; tissue repair and growth; secretion of endogenous opiates. The authors: "stress produces acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term) effects on variables including those listed in Table 8.4. There are many standard tests for and ways of observing most of the indicators of stress below; the thorough preparation of the athlete demands that they be applied regularly and appropriate restoration interventions be used" (PDF 457). Later they single out motor control: "careful attention has to be paid to changes in motor control or movement skill, since all sporting action relies fundamentally on muscle action controlled by the nervous system," which is why they earlier recommended "the coach making regular ratings of the technical perfection of the athlete's execution of important movements." "Quantitative measurement of individual indicators of motor proficiency, such as balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills, can also furnish useful data" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).
537	    17	
538	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for motor control: it applies even to "training which does not necessarily place great demands on qualities such as strength and endurance" (PDF 461), because all sporting action runs through the nervous system. Inference: a technique or coordination drop can show stress in skill-dominant athletes before strength or endurance tests move.
539	    19	
540	    20	**When to apply** — When choosing what to monitor, pick a few Table 8.4 functions that have a cheap test, and add one motor-control measure or a coach rating of technique. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: mRSI is a neuromuscular output measure; the book's list suggests reaction time or a coach technique rating as the complementary motor-control read.
541	    21	
542	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The table is a list of functions, not a validated battery; it gives no tests, norms or thresholds, and "applied regularly" is not defined. Several items (brain rhythms, endogenous opiates, pupil size) need laboratory access. The authors' own text slips: it calls the table "symptoms of overtraining stress" and also functions affected by stress in general.
543	    23	
544	    24	**Example** — The authors' motor-control battery: "balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills" (PDF 461 / p.450).

561	    14	# Colds and Minor Illness Under Prolonged Heavy Loading Mean Cut the Load and Add General Restoration Now
562	    15	
563	    16	**What it is** — The authors: "changes in the immune response (as reflected by the presence of colds and other apparently minor sicknesses) which accompany conditions of prolonged stressful loading, indicate the end of the general adaptation syndrome during the period of physical exhaustion, and the immediate need to decrease the loading and increase the amount of general restoration. This change in immune response is not necessarily directly associated with the physical loads, but may also relate strongly to increase in emotional stress, due, for instance, to the impending competitions or any other events involving large changes of psychological state. Timeous intervention is essential whenever the slightest hints of such disruptions in immune status become apparent" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image; the right margin is cut, so "accompany," "period of" and "restoration" are partly reconstructed).
564	    17	
565	    18	**Why it works** — The authors place the immune change at the exhaustion stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome, the point where adaptation reserves are used up (PDF 461; see 1.14 as cited in 8.5). Inference: a cold during a heavy block is then not bad luck but a late marker that the load has outrun adaptation, which is why the response is to cut load rather than train through.
566	    19	
567	    20	**When to apply** — When an athlete in a long, heavy block (or before a major competition) picks up colds or repeated minor illness, reduce the loading and add general restoration at once, and look at emotional stressors as well as training load. Table 8.3 lists "tendency to headaches, colds, fever blisters" under B-type overtraining (PDF 454 / p.443; see [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]]).
568	    21	
569	    22	**When NOT to apply** — No data are given; the link to the general adaptation syndrome is the authors' interpretation. A cold can come from exposure alone. Inference: the rule fits when illness coincides with "prolonged stressful loading"; an isolated cold in a light week is weak evidence of overload. Illness management itself belongs to medical staff, which the rule does not replace.
570	    23	
571	    24	**Example** — The authors' own non-training trigger: immune disruption "may also relate strongly to increase in emotional stress, due, for instance, to the impending competitions" (PDF 461 / p.450). Inference: a run of colds in the week before a rivalry game calls for less load even if the training plan has not changed.
572	    25	
573	    26	**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/claim--a-sleep-history-belongs-in-overtraining-screening]]

588	    14	# Makarova and Stupnitsky: Weekly Neuromuscular Screening Sorted Athletes Into Four Groups, Each With Its Own Restoration (Fig 8.4)
589	    15	
590	    16	**What it is** — The authors describe a year-long applied system (Makarova & Stupnitsky, 1983). For athletes with access to scientific institutes, neuromuscular system (NMS) state "may be assessed by methods such as monitoring of the quasi-stationary electrical potential of the brain, quantitative muscle palpation (using probes such as the myotonometer devised by Siff) and measurement of skin conductance or impedance at acupuncture points (Shishkin, 1989)." Makarova & Stupnitsky found that local muscle contraction (LMC) measured by tonometry "displays a clear topography and often coincides with the acupuncture points," and that "pronounced LMC" coincided "with a poorer functional state of the NMS," together with "increased muscle tonus, decreased strength, an increase in time for muscle relaxation and impaired rheographic indicators" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image). Over year-long programmes they saw "a characteristic change in the skin impedance whenever there is significant disruption in the athlete's adaptation," and used it, "sometimes assisted by other standard physiological tests (such as heart rate, blood pressure, flicker fusion rate in vision and reaction time)," to adjust training and restoration (PDF 461). Athletes were sorted by these indicators and their self-perception: Group I, "no disruptions in self-feeling, work capacity or NMS"; Group II, "minor local disturbances"; Group III, "definite complaints and muscle disturbances"; Group IV, "acute illnesses (colds etc.)" (PDF 461). "This diagnostic process was repeated once per weekly microcycle." Restoration went mainly to Groups II-IV, "with minimal application to those in Group I." Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures, with an arrow from the groups to Therapeutic Procedures; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation.
591	    17	
592	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' account: these indicators "point to a diminished work capacity" (PDF 461), so they can direct restoration to the athletes who need it and leave the rest alone. Inference: it is a triage system; Group I athletes get almost no restoration, consistent with the book's warning that routine restoration can blunt adaptation.
593	    19	
594	    20	**When to apply** — As a model for weekly triage: one screen per microcycle, a simple four-way sort (fine; local issue; general complaint; ill), and a different response for each, rather than one recovery routine for the roster.
595	    21	
596	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The book reports the design, not the outcomes; no numbers, sample size or comparison group are given, so `supported` rests only on a named, year-long applied study described in some detail. The measures (skin impedance at acupuncture points, quasi-stationary brain potential) are specialist and not standard practice. The text on PDF 461 refers the four groups to "(Fig 8.3)," but Fig 8.3 is the control-systems diagram on PDF 453; the restoration figure is Fig 8.4 on PDF 462. The text says Group II falls "between Groups I and III" while the group numbers suggest severity rises to IV; Group IV is illness, a different kind of state.
597	    23	
598	    24	**Example** — The weekly sort as the authors give it: Group II gets local reflexive procedures on the problem zones plus a little general restoration; Group IV gets mainly general restoration under medical supervision (PDF 462 / p.451).
599	    25

    14	# Six Strength-Training Causes of Overtraining Injury to Check First
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors' list: "In the case of strength training, overtraining injuries may be the result of too many repetitions or sets, regular training with near maximum loads, training the same muscle groups too frequently, inadequate recovery periods, insufficient rest or faulty execution of any movement" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image). Six causes: (1) too many repetitions or sets; (2) regular training with near-maximum loads; (3) training the same muscle groups too frequently; (4) inadequate recovery periods; (5) insufficient rest; (6) faulty execution of any movement.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The page gives the list without a mechanism. Inference: causes 1-5 are dose (volume, intensity, frequency, and recovery between and outside sessions) and cause 6 is technique, so the list splits a strength-room injury into "too much" versus "done wrong," which point to different fixes.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — As an audit sequence when a lifter develops an overuse complaint or a local overtraining picture (see [[heuristic--tell-general-from-local-overtraining-and-acute-from-chronic]]): check sets and reps, the share of near-maximal work, how often the same group is hit, rest between sessions, rest outside training, and technique. Eric's review: "Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 109, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: that maxim addresses causes 2 and 6 directly.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — No data, no thresholds and no ranking among the six; the list says what "may" cause injury. "Inadequate recovery periods" and "insufficient rest" overlap and the book does not separate them. The 8.2 discussion splits overtraining injuries into "overload injuries (caused by too large a load at any instant) and overuse injuries (caused by very frequent application of a given load)" (PDF 438 / p.427; see [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]]). Inference: cause 2 maps mainly to overload and causes 1 and 3 to overuse; the 8.5 list does not make that mapping itself.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Inference, applied: a lifter benching heavy four days a week who reports shoulder soreness that persists through rest days shows causes 2 and 3 at once; cutting near-maximal sessions to one and the bench frequency to two is the first test, before any treatment.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]], [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]]

    13	
    14	# Find the Optimum Stress Level Rather Than Avoiding Stress; Planned, Manageable Doses Build Tolerance
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Closing the overtraining discussion, the authors quote Selye: "The goal is certainly not to avoid stress - stress is a part of life. It is a natural by-product of all our activities .... But in order to express yourself fully, you must first find your optimum stress level and then use your adaptation energy at a rate and in a direction adjusted to the innate structure of your mind and body. It is not easy .... It takes much practice and almost constant self-analysis" (Selye, 1956). They read it as a definition of a programme: "a carefully designed sequence of physical and mental stresses in given conditioning workouts, with one's condition being constantly monitored and restoration being planned in a way and at a rate appropriate to one's current level of stress" (PDF 454 / p.443, checked against the page image). The same idea returns at the end of 8.6: "*Superadaptation* (supercompensation) or *innoculation* against specific stresses is possible by exposing yourself to properly structured doses of manageable stress," and "Very significantly, stress avoidance can make you more vulnerable to future stresses" (PDF 467 / p.456, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning on PDF 467: "The existence of supercompensatory processes implies that planned exposure to manageable stresses may enable one to cope with higher levels of stress" (item 12), and "Regular exposure to a stressor may produce either adaptation or sensitisation, so that the same level of stress may not produce the same response at a later stage" (item 10). Inference: avoidance gives no adaptation signal, so tolerance does not rise; too much gives sensitisation instead of adaptation; the target is the dose between.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When deciding how much to protect an athlete from load. Eric's review: "Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 40, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: Eric's "culture of fear" point and the authors' "stress avoidance can make you more vulnerable" make the same argument against under-loading. The authors' own requirement is the second half of the sentence: condition "constantly monitored" and restoration planned to the current stress.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Selye's quote is a general life principle from 1956, not a training study; the authors offer no data that stress avoidance raises vulnerability in athletes. "Optimum" is not defined; item 9 on PDF 467 itself says "The concept of stress optimisation is not always accurate." The principle does not license loading through the warning signs in 8.5 (see [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own definition of an effective programme, quoted above, ends with restoration "planned in a way and at a rate appropriate to one's current level of stress" (PDF 454 / p.443): load and restoration are dosed together, not one after the other.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]], [[principle--prepare-athletes-for-risky-movements-instead-of-avoiding-them]], [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]

    13	
    14	# Restoration Is Planned Into Training and Is Not Rehabilitation; Most Rehabilitation Follows Failed Pedagogical Restoration
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors open 8.6: "Restoration is an integral part of overall training and practice, so that it must be applied with the short-term and long-term goals constantly in mind. A comprehensive training programme alternates different training techniques with situationally appropriate restorative means." The distinction: "*restoration* in training and competition is not synonymous with *rehabilitation*, which refers to the treatment of overtraining, illness or injury" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). They return to it on the next page: "Restoration is an integral part of the overall training programme, planned to fit in at the most effective and appropriate stages of training. Rehabilitation refers to therapy to restore an injured athlete to full functional capability. Very often the need for rehabilitation is the consequence of inadequate restoration, especially imperfect pedagogical restoration, i.e. a training schedule which produces overtraining" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' causal claim is in the last sentence: a schedule that overtrains creates the injuries that then need rehabilitation. "Although accidents can happen which are largely outside the control of the athlete, the essence of training is to maximise performance and minimise injuries, pain and soreness" (PDF 456). Inference: on this view, restoration is a planning job owned by whoever writes the training, while rehabilitation is a treatment job, so a rise in rehab caseload is first a question about the programme.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When rehab cases cluster, audit the training schedule ("pedagogical restoration") before adding treatments. When planning, put restoration in the plan at set stages rather than leaving it to the athlete's request. Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: Eric's load-design approach is what the authors call pedagogical restoration; the book's other two classes (medico-biological and psychological, see [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]]) have no counterpart in the baseline.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — "Very often" is not quantified and no injury data are given. The authors also say "Full restoration can sometimes be undesirable" and that "some Russian experts emphasize the importance of periodically training on a basis of *non-recovery* (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 455), so integral restoration does not mean full recovery between every session (see [[heuristic--incomplete-restoration-workouts-zalessky-rules]]). Accidents fall outside the claim by the authors' own words.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' description of top Russian practice: "It is not unusual for top Russian athletes to receive over an hour of restoration every day, with regular alternation of individualised methods and periodic training superimposed on a state of non-restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[principle--return-to-play-incomplete-until-the-athlete-perceives-full-healing]], [[heuristic--six-strength-training-causes-of-overtraining-injury]], [[principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random]]

    13	
    14	# Rotate Restorative Means: The Same Form at Most Once or Twice a Week, and a Day Off After Two Days of a Local Procedure
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors report the Russian dosing rule: "With prolonged use of any given means of restoration, the recuperative effect decreases, so that Russian experts usually recommend that the same restorative means should not be applied more than once or twice a week in the same form. They consider that, in applying local-effect procedures, it is advisable to have a single day's break after every two days of application. In particular, the body adapts more rapidly to local-effect restorative means than to general restorative means (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). They add that no single modality is enough: "Massage is not enough, saunas are part of the picture, reflexology is limited; all individual modalities are insufficient to guarantee optimal restoration in modern sport" (PDF 455). Later they restate it as "a recurrent theme throughout this book, namely that overuse of any technique leads to eventual ineffectiveness," and cite "a *complementarity effect* produced by the integrated use of several restorative means and methods carefully introduced at specific stages of a training programme" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is habituation: the body adapts to a repeated restorative stimulus, faster to local than to general means, so its effect fades (PDF 455). Inference: this is the same accommodation logic the book applies to training means, where a means loses effect with repeated use and must be replaced.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a team uses one recovery modality daily (the same massage, the same contrast bath, the same compression device), rotate forms through the week, and after two consecutive days of a local procedure on the same area, skip a day. Eric's review: "Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the rotation rule gives a dosing limit for the technology Eric already treats as secondary.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The rule is cited to Siff & Yessis (1992) with no study data on these pages; the numbers (once or twice a week, one day off after two) are expert recommendations. "In the same form" leaves open how different two forms must be to count as different. Inference: the habituation claim concerns restorative effect, not safety; it is not a reason to stop a medically prescribed treatment.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The Soviet track cycling programme applied the rule across the year: "Because the same restorative means diminish their effectiveness when they are used over prolonged periods, the restorative means were alternated, regarding both content and volume, depending on the stage of the annual cycle" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image; see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]]

    13	
    14	# Train on Incomplete Restoration Only for 2-3 Days, in a Healthy Athlete, With Full Restoration and Medical Cover After
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors: "It may also be inappropriate to routinely apply restoration on a frequent basis, since increase in work capacity can be stimulated by using workouts which are specially calculated to produce incomplete restoration." This is done by "prescribing some individual sessions which are especially demanding for some body zones or processes or the use of several sessions per day for a limited period" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image; the scan's right margin is cut on this page and the words "capacity" and "processes" are partly reconstructed). The authors cite Kopysov (1980) for the recommendation of "Some authorities" that in the period immediately before competitions, "especially in the strength and power sports," it is often advisable to run intense workouts with minimal restoration "unless there are very clear indications" that it is needed (PDF 461, paraphrased across clipped words). Zalessky's (1980) rules for "all *incomplete restoration* workouts": "The athlete should be completely healthy and in good functional state"; "Incomplete restoration should not last for more than 2-3 days"; "After such workout phases, all means should be used to facilitate full restoration"; "Medical guidance or assistance should always be available during such phases" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that work capacity can be stimulated by planned under-recovery (PDF 461), echoing the 8.6 opening that "Full restoration can sometimes be undesirable" (PDF 455 / p.444). Inference: the four rules bound the risk of that stimulus, so a short overreach is followed by a full rebound instead of sliding into the accumulated imbalance the book calls overtraining.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When planning a deliberate overreach (a shock microcycle, several sessions per day for a short block, or a pre-competition phase in a strength or power sport), check all four of Zalessky's conditions and schedule the full-restoration phase before the block starts.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Not in an athlete who is ill, injured or already showing overtraining signs (the first rule). Not for longer than 2-3 days. Not without access to medical help; Inference: in a college setting that means Athletic Medicine is told before the block. Kopysov's minimal-restoration advice is stated for "the strength and power sports"; the book does not extend it to team sports. No study data are given for any of the rules.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' two ways of creating incomplete restoration: sessions "especially demanding for some body zones" or "several sessions per day for a limited period" (PDF 461 / p.450). Inference: a two-day block of twice-daily lower-body sessions before a deload week fits both the method and the 2-3 day limit.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]], [[heuristic--shock-microcycle-limits]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]]

     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "8.6"

    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Three Classes of Restoration: Pedagogical (Coaching), Medico-Biological and Psychological, Plus Natural Recovery Outside Training
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "The Russians usually recognise three classes of restoration (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456 / p.445, checked against the page image):
    17	- *Pedagogical (coaching) restoration* "employs carefully periodised programmes to optimise the balance between training stresses and natural recuperative processes." It includes "combinational training, known in the West as 'cross training'," active rest, and "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities" after "demanding strength training sessions." Micro-, meso- and macrocycles, with the preparatory period split into General and Special Physical Preparation, exist "specifically to promote supercompensation via suitable phasing of loading and restoration regimes (see Ch 6)."
    18	- *Medico-biological restoration* covers "therapeutic measures offered by medical and allied practitioners," sometimes split into physiotherapeutic and pharmacological measures. Physical measures divide into natural means ("massage, showers, heat, sunlight and training outdoors") and additional means ("electrostimulation, electrosleep, diathermy, acupuncture, baro-chambers, laser therapy and ultrasound").
    19	- *Psychological restoration* "involves management of the mental state": hypnosis, self-hypnosis, auto-suggestion, autogenics, visualisation, progressive relaxation, guided imagery, music therapy and learning techniques, some using biofeedback or electrodermal devices.
    20	Beyond these, "it is essential to encourage natural recovery relating to family, living conditions, lifestyle, nutrition, leisure activities, beneficial socialisation, team atmosphere, work conditions, spiritual needs and coaching team interaction" (PDF 456). A later restatement (PDF 458 / p.447, read from the page image) puts pedagogical methods "outside the scope of this text" and splits the rest into physical, medical and psychological means. Table 8.5 subdivides them: physical (passive, active, combined); medical (pharmacological, psychiatric, surgical, nutritional, combined); psychological (therapist-administered, self-administered, combined). Table 8.6 lists physical means in three columns, active means mainly in the last (for example physical activity, recreational sport, manual labour, dance, play, postural realignment, breathing regimens, progressive relaxation, Tai Chi, yoga); Table 8.7 lists 14 psychological means from psychotherapy to "Laughter/tears" (PDF 459 / p.448).
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the system is its specificity: "The Russian restoration system recognises the *specificity of each technique or sequence of techniques* for a particular sport, phase of training, individual athlete, time of the day, type of stress and type of fitness," applied "before, during, shortly after and a long time after training and competitions," with "Meticulous records" of daily physical and psychological state (PDF 456). On natural recovery: "problems which lie outside the training setting can easily predominate over training problems in determining the success of the athlete in competition" (PDF 456).
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — As a coverage check on a recovery plan: is there a pedagogical element (load phasing, active rest), a medico-biological element (by whom), a psychological element, and attention to life outside training? The authors also note that "the athlete is encouraged to shed dependence on the therapist and to learn *self-restoration* procedures (Siff & Yessis, 1992)" (PDF 456). Eric's review: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: by the book's scheme that is the pedagogical class only.
    25	
    26	**When NOT to apply** — The categories are descriptive; the authors say Table 8.5 "should not be regarded as definitive or exclusive" (PDF 458). The lists mix well-studied means with ones that have little support (for example "Religion," "Screaming/shouting" in Table 8.7; "Therapeutic Touch," "Aromatherapy" in Table 8.6); inclusion is not endorsement of effect. Inference: the medico-biological class includes pharmacological means; anything in that class sits with the medical staff, not the strength coach.
    27	
    28	**Example** — The pedagogical example the authors give: "Low intensity cyclical, rhythmical, circulatory or cardiovascular activities can also be very useful for promoting recovery after demanding strength training sessions" (PDF 456 / p.445).
    29	
    30	**Related** — [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]], [[framework--restoration-prescription-checklist-and-means-versus-methods]], [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]], [[browns-strength-and-conditioning-2008--myslinski/heuristic--restoration-emphasis-rises-as-the-off-season-advances]]
