     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "8.6"
     7	topic: placebo and rapport
     8	category: [restoration, placebo, psychology, therapy, belief]
     9	confidence: untested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Belief and Rapport Carry Much of a Restoration Technique's Effect, Which Is Both a Tool and a Confound
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors: "Certainly, many of these techniques may work because they are placebos, because the user believes in them. Yet, this is a very good reason not to dismiss them." If the mind can be focused "by an apparently illogical or foolish concept to perform unusual feats of performance or healing, then it is vital that we uncover the underlying physiological principles which make the *placebo effect* (or 'faith factor') so powerful. Placebos can produce positive and negative effects; it is up to science to sift the useful from the harmful" (PDF 455 / p.444, checked against the page image). The same effect "can also confound the validity of many restoration techniques, which work not because of any special merits, but because the practitioner persuades the user of its value." Hence "Virtually every claim by one massage therapist will be countered by another 'expert'" (PDF 455). On rapport: "the therapy often succeeds because of the rapport between therapist and client," and in sports restoration "*The rapport between you and the athlete is central to the success of the therapy*. In short, the belief of the athlete in you and your therapy (and sometimes an outside force, depending on the athlete's belief system) is an integral part of successful restoration" (PDF 456 / p.445, italics in the original, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "physical and mental healing are inextricably linked," so "one cannot separate the therapy from the therapist" (PDF 456). They draw the research consequence: "great care has to be taken to choose experimental and control groups and to exclude as far as possible all confounding factors such as the placebo effect and human interaction" (PDF 456). The 8.6 closing list makes the same point as propositions: "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it," and a technique "obtained at high cost," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or that "appeals to the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user is more likely to succeed" (items 1-4, PDF 467 / p.456).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Two uses. Practice: before using any restoration means, "consider the background and attitudes of the athlete, because these factors can have a profound effect on the efficacy of any regime" (PDF 458 / p.447). Evaluation: when a staff member reports that a modality works, ask whether the comparison controlled for belief and attention. Inference: Eric's account of abandoned wellness surveys, where athletes learned what answers the survey rewarded (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89), is a reminder that self-report after a treatment carries the same bias.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — These are the authors' opinions; no placebo-controlled data are given here. Two pages later the authors push the other way: "This [sic] is sometimes a tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," which their Russian research summary is meant "to correct" (PDF 465 / p.454; see [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]]). The two positions are not a contradiction in the book's own terms: belief adds to some real effects, and confounds the rest. Using belief deliberately raises an honesty question the book does not address.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: "one therapist will swear that aromatherapy with a certain fragrance will help, while another may claim the opposite. Another will extol the virtue of deep transverse friction for adhesions, whereas yet another will have equal success with therapeutic touch" (PDF 455 / p.444).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[framework--eighteen-propositions-on-sport-science-and-stress-management]], [[heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]]
##### FILE: framework--restoration-prescription-checklist-and-means-versus-methods.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "8.6"
     7	topic: restoration prescription
     8	category: [restoration, therapy, stress-management, checklist, prescription]
     9	confidence: untested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Prescribe Restoration Like a Drug: Ten Prescription Features, Twelve Stress Factors, Eight P-Factors, Five Questions, Then Means Before Methods
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under "Application of Restoration Measures" the authors set a four-step checklist (PDF 457 / p.446, checked against the page image):
    17	1. Features of therapeutic prescription to understand first: indications; contraindications; effects; side-effects; dosage; directions for use; special precautions; symptoms of misuse; treatment of misuse; dependence on therapy.
    18	2. Effects to analyse on the person under stress: perception of the stress and its effects; attitude towards the stress; sensory input associated with it; motor activity and its effect on it; response of body and mind; "Hierarchies of stresses acting at any instant"; intensity or quality; volume or quantity; density or concentration; duration; onset; causes.
    19	3. Factors to examine "before undertaking any form of therapy": procedures (types of therapy); purpose of therapy; person; practitioner; place; period; position; pain/pleasure.
    20	4. Questions: "Is it - Appropriate, Effective, Sufficient, Safe, Enjoyable?"
    21	Then: "Once you have applied this checklist, you may now select the appropriate restoration means and methods for a given person at a given time." The two terms differ: "The *means* refers to the broad general type of restoration measure (e.g. massage), whereas the *method* refers to that specific technique chosen (e.g. kneading massage) which falls within that means" (PDF 457 / p.446).
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — The authors' premise: restoration techniques, "like any other therapies," must be prescribed with an understanding of these features (PDF 457). Inference: listing misuse, dependence and side-effects alongside effects treats a recovery modality as a dose with a cost, which is the point the book makes elsewhere about routine restoration blunting adaptation.
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — Before adding any recovery modality to a team routine, or when an athlete asks for one. The checklist parallels the authors' P-factor checklist for exercise prescription in 8.3 (see [[framework--exercise-checklist-and-nine-p-factors-of-exercise-prescription]]). Inference: "Dependence on therapy" is the item most often skipped in practice, and it links to the authors' aim that athletes learn self-restoration.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — The checklist is a list of headings without criteria; it tells the practitioner what to consider, not what to decide. It gives no order of priority among the 35 items. Inference: in a team setting, steps 2 and 3 are only practical for individual cases, not for roster-wide routines. The means/methods distinction is terminological; it does not imply that methods within a means are interchangeable.
    28	
    29	**Example** — The authors' own: massage is a *means*; kneading massage is a *method* within it (PDF 457 / p.446). Table 8.8 then lists 20 massage methods within that one means (PDF 459 / p.448; see [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]]).
    30	
    31	**Related** — [[framework--exercise-checklist-and-nine-p-factors-of-exercise-prescription]], [[framework--three-classes-of-restoration-pedagogical-medico-biological-psychological]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]] (perception of stress)
##### FILE: framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "8.6"
     7	topic: stress indicators
     8	category: [monitoring, overtraining, stress, motor-control, readiness]
     9	confidence: untested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# What Stress Changes (Table 8.4), and Why Motor Control Belongs on the Monitoring List
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Table 8.4, "Functions affected by physiological and psychological stress," introduced as "some of the symptoms of overtraining stress" (PDF 456 / p.445), lists 20 functions in three columns (PDF 457 / p.446, read from the page image): heart rate; blood pressure; muscular tension; muscle irritability; pain threshold; brain rhythms; breathing patterns; sleep patterns; body temperature; concentration and alertness; digestion, gastric acidity; endocrine secretion; immune response; fine motor control; reaction time; posture; pupil size (of the eye); general irritability, mood, stability; tissue repair and growth; secretion of endogenous opiates. The authors: "stress produces acute (short-term) and chronic (long-term) effects on variables including those listed in Table 8.4. There are many standard tests for and ways of observing most of the indicators of stress below; the thorough preparation of the athlete demands that they be applied regularly and appropriate restoration interventions be used" (PDF 457). Later they single out motor control: "careful attention has to be paid to changes in motor control or movement skill, since all sporting action relies fundamentally on muscle action controlled by the nervous system," which is why they earlier recommended "the coach making regular ratings of the technical perfection of the athlete's execution of important movements." "Quantitative measurement of individual indicators of motor proficiency, such as balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills, can also furnish useful data" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for motor control: it applies even to "training which does not necessarily place great demands on qualities such as strength and endurance" (PDF 461), because all sporting action runs through the nervous system. Inference: a technique or coordination drop can show stress in skill-dominant athletes before strength or endurance tests move.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When choosing what to monitor, pick a few Table 8.4 functions that have a cheap test, and add one motor-control measure or a coach rating of technique. Eric's review: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: mRSI is a neuromuscular output measure; the book's list suggests reaction time or a coach technique rating as the complementary motor-control read.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The table is a list of functions, not a validated battery; it gives no tests, norms or thresholds, and "applied regularly" is not defined. Several items (brain rhythms, endogenous opiates, pupil size) need laboratory access. The authors' own text slips: it calls the table "symptoms of overtraining stress" and also functions affected by stress in general.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' motor-control battery: "balancing tests, reaction time, movement speed in prescribed actions, coordination, and eye-hand, eye-foot and eye-object skills" (PDF 461 / p.450).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]], [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]], [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]], [[case-study--makarova-stupnitsky-weekly-four-group-restoration-triage-fig-8-4]], [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]
##### FILE: heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: heuristic
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "8.6"
     7	topic: immune warning sign
     8	category: [monitoring, immune, overtraining, illness, restoration]
     9	confidence: untested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Colds and Minor Illness Under Prolonged Heavy Loading Mean Cut the Load and Add General Restoration Now
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors: "changes in the immune response (as reflected by the presence of colds and other apparently minor sicknesses) which accompany conditions of prolonged stressful loading, indicate the end of the general adaptation syndrome during the period of physical exhaustion, and the immediate need to decrease the loading and increase the amount of general restoration. This change in immune response is not necessarily directly associated with the physical loads, but may also relate strongly to increase in emotional stress, due, for instance, to the impending competitions or any other events involving large changes of psychological state. Timeous intervention is essential whenever the slightest hints of such disruptions in immune status become apparent" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image; the right margin is cut, so "accompany," "period of" and "restoration" are partly reconstructed).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors place the immune change at the exhaustion stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome, the point where adaptation reserves are used up (PDF 461; see 1.14 as cited in 8.5). Inference: a cold during a heavy block is then not bad luck but a late marker that the load has outrun adaptation, which is why the response is to cut load rather than train through.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When an athlete in a long, heavy block (or before a major competition) picks up colds or repeated minor illness, reduce the loading and add general restoration at once, and look at emotional stressors as well as training load. Table 8.3 lists "tendency to headaches, colds, fever blisters" under B-type overtraining (PDF 454 / p.443; see [[framework--a-and-b-overtraining-addisonic-and-basedowic-table-8-3]]).
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — No data are given; the link to the general adaptation syndrome is the authors' interpretation. A cold can come from exposure alone. Inference: the rule fits when illness coincides with "prolonged stressful loading"; an isolated cold in a light week is weak evidence of overload. Illness management itself belongs to medical staff, which the rule does not replace.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own non-training trigger: immune disruption "may also relate strongly to increase in emotional stress, due, for instance, to the impending competitions" (PDF 461 / p.450). Inference: a run of colds in the week before a rivalry game calls for less load even if the training plan has not changed.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/claim--a-sleep-history-belongs-in-overtraining-screening]]
##### FILE: case-study--makarova-stupnitsky-weekly-four-group-restoration-triage-fig-8-4.md
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: case-study
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "8.6"
     7	topic: restoration triage
     8	category: [restoration, monitoring, neuromuscular, triage, microcycle]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-13
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Makarova and Stupnitsky: Weekly Neuromuscular Screening Sorted Athletes Into Four Groups, Each With Its Own Restoration (Fig 8.4)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors describe a year-long applied system (Makarova & Stupnitsky, 1983). For athletes with access to scientific institutes, neuromuscular system (NMS) state "may be assessed by methods such as monitoring of the quasi-stationary electrical potential of the brain, quantitative muscle palpation (using probes such as the myotonometer devised by Siff) and measurement of skin conductance or impedance at acupuncture points (Shishkin, 1989)." Makarova & Stupnitsky found that local muscle contraction (LMC) measured by tonometry "displays a clear topography and often coincides with the acupuncture points," and that "pronounced LMC" coincided "with a poorer functional state of the NMS," together with "increased muscle tonus, decreased strength, an increase in time for muscle relaxation and impaired rheographic indicators" (PDF 461 / p.450, checked against the page image). Over year-long programmes they saw "a characteristic change in the skin impedance whenever there is significant disruption in the athlete's adaptation," and used it, "sometimes assisted by other standard physiological tests (such as heart rate, blood pressure, flicker fusion rate in vision and reaction time)," to adjust training and restoration (PDF 461). Athletes were sorted by these indicators and their self-perception: Group I, "no disruptions in self-feeling, work capacity or NMS"; Group II, "minor local disturbances"; Group III, "definite complaints and muscle disturbances"; Group IV, "acute illnesses (colds etc.)" (PDF 461). "This diagnostic process was repeated once per weekly microcycle." Restoration went mainly to Groups II-IV, "with minimal application to those in Group I." Group II received "point-reflexive and local reflexive procedures focusing on the problematic body zones," with "a small amount of general restoration"; in Group IV "general restoration means predominated over lesser used local reflexive methods," with the rehabilitative process "under medical supervision" (PDF 461-462 / p.450-451). Fig 8.4, "Organisation of the systems of restoration for athletes," read from the figure as far as its arrows can be traced (PDF 462 / p.451): Evaluation of the Functional State, linked to Consideration of Current Condition, feeds Groups I-IV; Groups II-IV feed Restorative Procedures, with an arrow from the groups to Therapeutic Procedures; Group I and Restorative Procedures feed the Training Process, which loops back to evaluation.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' account: these indicators "point to a diminished work capacity" (PDF 461), so they can direct restoration to the athletes who need it and leave the rest alone. Inference: it is a triage system; Group I athletes get almost no restoration, consistent with the book's warning that routine restoration can blunt adaptation.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — As a model for weekly triage: one screen per microcycle, a simple four-way sort (fine; local issue; general complaint; ill), and a different response for each, rather than one recovery routine for the roster.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The book reports the design, not the outcomes; no numbers, sample size or comparison group are given, so `supported` rests only on a named, year-long applied study described in some detail. The measures (skin impedance at acupuncture points, quasi-stationary brain potential) are specialist and not standard practice. The text on PDF 461 refers the four groups to "(Fig 8.3)," but Fig 8.3 is the control-systems diagram on PDF 453; the restoration figure is Fig 8.4 on PDF 462. The text says Group II falls "between Groups I and III" while the group numbers suggest severity rises to IV; Group IV is illness, a different kind of state.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The weekly sort as the authors give it: Group II gets local reflexive procedures on the problem zones plus a little general restoration; Group IV gets mainly general restoration under medical supervision (PDF 462 / p.451).

600	    26	**Related** — [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]], [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]]
601	##### FILE: case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours.md
602	     1	---
603	     2	type: library-entry
604	     3	kind: case-study
605	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
606	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
607	     6	chapter: "8.6"
608	     7	topic: restoration timing study
609	     8	category: [restoration, recovery, sauna, hydrotherapy, timing, supercompensation]
610	     9	confidence: supported
611	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
612	    11	created: 2026-10-13
613	    12	---
614	    13	
615	    14	# Talyshev: Sauna Plus Hydrotherapy Right After a Workout Helped That Day but Hurt the Next; 6-9 Hours Later It Produced Supercompensation
616	    15	
617	    16	**What it is** — Talyshev (1977) "conducted research on a large group of highly qualified athletes who followed a standardised training programme. Following a workout, the athletes took a sauna in combination with hydrotherapy - in one case directly after the workout; in the other cases, 3, 6, and 9 hours later, accompanied by a large battery of physiological tests" (PDF 462 / p.451, checked against the page image). Results as reported:
618	    17	- No baths or hydrotherapy: work capacity "dropped sharply immediately after the workout," and "noticeable recovery commenced on the following day."
619	    18	- Immediately after: "a marked increase in work capacity immediately following the therapy and 3 hours later. However, this increase slowed down, and work capacity did not recover and even fell below its initial level on the following day."
620	    19	- At 3 hours: "a pronounced increase in work capacity 6 hours after the therapy (9 hours after the workout). Work capacity returned to its initial level on the following day."
621	    20	- At 6, "and especially 9 hours": "work capacity not only recovered on the following day, but there was significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451).
622	    21	
623	    22	**Why it works** — The setup in the book: "The highest intensity and rate of recovery is observed immediately upon cessation of exercise, after which it diminishes gradually (Talyshev, 1977). Logically, *it is more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down*" (PDF 462, italics in the original). The book frames recovery in three phases (Zalessky, 1979): "On-going recovery" during activity; "Rapid recovery" immediately after, "leading to removal of metabolic by-products and replenishment of depleted energy resources"; and "Delayed recovery, which surpasses the initial level if training loads are not excessive" (PDF 455 / p.444). Inference: an intervention during the rapid phase adds little to a process already running fast and may cut short the signal; one in the delayed phase supports the process when it slows.
624	    23	
625	    24	**When to apply** — As evidence for timing heat and water therapies by the next performance demand, not by habit (see [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]]).
626	    25	
627	    26	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample size, no measure of "work capacity," no statistics and no control for the order of conditions; "large group of highly qualified athletes" is all that is said. The result is for sauna plus hydrotherapy; it says nothing on its own about massage, cold or compression. The "no therapy" condition is described only qualitatively, so the supercompensation at 6-9 hours is not compared numerically with it.
628	    27	
629	    28	**Example** — The study's sharpest contrast: therapy straight after the workout left next-day work capacity "below its initial level," while the same therapy 9 hours later produced next-day "significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451).
630	    29	
631	    30	**Related** — [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]
632	##### FILE: heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed.md
633	     1	---
634	     2	type: library-entry
635	     3	kind: heuristic
636	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
637	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
638	     6	chapter: "8.6"
639	     7	topic: restoration timing
640	     8	category: [restoration, recovery, timing, two-a-days, competition]
641	     9	confidence: supported
642	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
643	    11	created: 2026-10-13
644	    12	---
645	    13	
646	    14	# Time Restoration to When Work Capacity Is Next Needed: Immediately for the Same Day, 6-9 Hours Later for Tomorrow; Whole-Body After General Work, Local After Local
647	    15	
648	    16	**What it is** — Talyshev's (1977) conclusion from his timing study: "work capacity and its magnitude depend strongly on the time at which the restorative methods are applied. When an immediate effect is necessary, namely when the greatest work capacity recovery after a short span of time is needed (e.g. between morning and afternoon workouts), it is advisable to employ restorative methods immediately after workouts or morning starts. If, however, a high work capacity is required on the following day, then it is better to employ recovery methods 6-9 hours after the workout or competition. If the workout or competition ends late in the evening, it is preferable to start recovery procedures in the morning, shortly after awakening" (PDF 462 / p.451, checked against the page image). A second rule from "Related work": "it is best to employ full-body recovery methods (e.g. sauna, hydrotherapy, general massage) after large volume of general training work. In contrast, local methods (e.g. pressure methods, local manual or vibrational massage, local heating) are preferable following the execution of work which strongly stresses specific muscle groups" (PDF 462).
649	    17	
650	    18	**Why it works** — The basis is the study (see [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]): immediate therapy raised work capacity for a few hours but left it below baseline the next day, while therapy at 6-9 hours produced next-day supercompensation (PDF 462). The authors' framing: recovery is fastest straight after exercise, so it is "more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down" (PDF 462).
651	    19	
652	    20	**When to apply** — Two-a-days and tournaments: restoration straight after the first session. Normal training days with the next key session tomorrow: restoration in the evening, roughly 6-9 hours after training, or the next morning if training ended late. Choose whole-body means after high-volume general work and local means after work that hammered one muscle group. Eric's review: "Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)). Inference: the baseline schedules recovery by day; the book's rule would add a time-of-day decision inside the day.
653	    21	
654	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The data come from one study of sauna with hydrotherapy in highly qualified athletes, reported without numbers (see the case study). The whole-body versus local rule is cited only as "Related work," and the authors concede it is "still fairly general and the question remains as to how does the dosage of a specific recovery method relates to the severity of the training load" (PDF 462). Inference: in a game week where the priority is the game, not adaptation, the immediate option may be right even for next-day readiness; the book does not address that trade-off.
655	    23	
656	    24	**Example** — The authors' own case for immediate use: "between morning and afternoon workouts" (PDF 462 / p.451). Their case for delay: a workout or competition ending late in the evening, with recovery started "in the morning, shortly after awakening."
657	    25	
658	    26	**Related** — [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules]]
659	##### FILE: heuristic--judge-restoration-by-performance-and-injuries-and-test-it-under-sport-loads.md
660	     1	---
661	     2	type: library-entry
662	     3	kind: heuristic
663	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
664	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
665	     6	chapter: "8.6"
666	     7	topic: evaluating restoration
667	     8	category: [restoration, evaluation, monitoring, records, injury]
668	     9	confidence: untested
669	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
670	    11	created: 2026-10-13
671	    12	---
672	    13	
673	    14	# Judge a Restoration Method by Performance and Injuries, Not Client Feeling, and Test It Under Sport-Typical Loads
674	    15	
675	    16	**What it is** — Two rules for evaluating restoration. First: "Client feeling and appreciation are not enough; in sports restoration, the basic indicators are improved performance and fewer injuries." The reader should "experiment with variations, to keep records and to devise recipes which consistently yield successful results" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image). Second, from Talyshev (1977): because "it is very difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of specific recovery method," it "is more advisable to test the effectiveness of a specific recovery method by using test loads that approximate most closely the natural training conditions, by using loads in sports exercises that are typically encountered in a given sport" (PDF 460-461 / p.449-450, checked against the page images).
676	    17	
677	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for caution: "if certain recovery methods are employed after a workout, then the positive after-effects (or training effect) stimulated by the workout tend to be negated," so "the unskilled use of recovery methods can markedly increase the amount of training work and yet not provide a corresponding training effect" (PDF 460 / p.449). Inference: an athlete can feel better and train more while adapting less, so feeling and session volume are the wrong outcome measures; performance and injury rate capture the net effect.
678	    19	
679	    20	**When to apply** — When a modality is adopted or kept, write down what outcome it is meant to change, track performance and injuries across its use, and test it with the sport's own loads (for example a repeated-sprint or practice-like session) rather than a lab task. Eric's review: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89, Explicit). Inference: the same distrust of self-report that ended the surveys applies to "this feels good" as evidence for a recovery tool.
680	    21	
681	    22	**When NOT to apply** — Performance and injury rate are slow, noisy outcomes; Inference: with a small group they cannot separate one modality's effect within a season, so the rule supports keeping records over time rather than quick verdicts. The book gives no example of a method that was dropped under this rule. Feeling still matters for adherence and is part of the placebo effect the authors elsewhere call useful (see [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]]).
682	    23	
683	    24	**Example** — The authors' framing of Russian work: "systematic use of recovery methods makes it possible to significantly and sometimes rapidly increase the volume and intensity of training while simultaneously decreasing the incidence of musculoskeletal injuries" (PDF 460 / p.449), which names the two outcomes, training capacity and injuries, they want restoration judged on.
684	    25	
685	    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]]
686	##### FILE: principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random.md
687	     1	---
688	     2	type: library-entry
689	     3	kind: principle
690	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
691	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
692	     6	chapter: "8.6"
693	     7	topic: periodised restoration
694	     8	category: [restoration, periodisation, recovery, planning]
695	     9	confidence: untested
696	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
697	    11	created: 2026-10-13
698	    12	---
699	    13	
700	    14	# Periodise Restoration in Complexes Tied to the Training Stage; Do Not Apply It at Random or Because the Athlete Feels Tired
701	    15	
702	    16	**What it is** — Under "Complexes and Periodisation in Restoration": "The tendency to apply restorative means and methods largely at random, depending on one's preferences and training, should be avoided, since different processes or body components (nervous, muscular, ligamentous, metabolic, psychological, cardiovascular etc.) fatigue, recover and adapt at different rates and to different degrees, depending on the nature of the loading and the athlete. The value of combining, complexing and periodising training loads according to individualised programmes has achieved a high degree of acceptance, but the value of a similar approach in restoration often tends to be ignored" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image). Because manual methods cannot be given volumes and intensities like training loads, "one more frequently refers to the use of restorative complexes or of periodised training programmes which incorporate restorative procedures" (PDF 463). The failure the authors name: "inappropriate timing can delay or even reverse recovery after training, yet many well-meaning therapists quite casually employ massage, spinal manipulation, electrostimulation, hydrotherapy and other common methods simply because the athlete feels 'tired', sore, stressed or unmotivated" (PDF 463).
703	    17	
704	    18	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is differential recovery: tissues and systems recover at different rates, so one routine applied at random will be early for some and late for others (PDF 463). Inference: grouping means into complexes matched to a training stage lets the restoration target the system that the stage loads most.
705	    19	
706	    20	**When to apply** — When writing the annual plan, write the restoration plan alongside it: which complex in which stage, and what changes as the stage changes. Treat "the athlete feels tired" as a cue to check the plan, not as an order for a treatment.
707	    21	
708	    22	**When NOT to apply** — No outcome data here; the authors defer "A more thorough exposition" to Siff & Yessis (1992) and give one example (PDF 463). Inference: this principle concerns planned restoration; it does not forbid responding to an injury or an acute medical need, which the book places under rehabilitation.
709	    23	
710	    24	**Example** — The book's worked example is the Soviet track cycling team's five-year programme, where the restorative means were "closely linked to the objectives of the individual stages of training" (PDF 463 / p.452; see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]).
711	    25	
712	    26	**Related** — [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]], [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]], [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[browns-strength-and-conditioning-2008--myslinski/heuristic--restoration-emphasis-rises-as-the-off-season-advances]]
713	##### FILE: case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11.md
714	     1	---
715	     2	type: library-entry
716	     3	kind: case-study
717	     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
718	     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
719	     6	chapter: "8.6"
720	     7	topic: periodised restoration programme
721	     8	category: [restoration, periodisation, cycling, microcycle, massage, hydrotherapy]
722	     9	confidence: untested
723	    10	ingest-tier: full-text
724	    11	created: 2026-10-13
725	    12	---
726	    13	
727	    14	# Soviet Track Cycling: Three Groups of Restorative Means Matched to Each Training Stage, and a Shock Microcycle With Restoration Twice a Day (Table 8.11)
728	    15	
729	    16	**What it is** — "The Soviet track cycling team, for a period of 5 years, successfully used this type of programme of restoration, (Goletz & Osadchy, 1986)," with three groups of means: "Group 1 (Basic means) for rapidly eliminating the fatigue following a training session"; "Group 2 (On-going means) for restoring the individual components of athletic preparedness to elevate the work capacity of these components during subsequent training sessions"; "Group 3 (Operative means) for stimulating work capacity directly before or during a workout or competition" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image). By stage:
730	    17	- *General base-building*: "only *basic* type restorative means," because the stage has "concentrated, high-volume workloads." At the end of the microcycle, before a rest day: a hydro session or short gentle swim, restorative massage, warm baths with essences (pine, eucalyptus, sea salt), and a hot-cold contrast bath or shower (PDF 463).
731	    18	- *Progressing training*: basic and on-going means per the microcycle plan, adding localised manual massage, showers and light therapy; at microcycle end, hydro procedures with electrotherapy, electromagnetic fields, ultrasound and barometric techniques (PDF 463).
732	    19	- *Winter indoor competitions*: more "non-relaxing *operative* means." Sprint and heat groups: "brisk pre-start massage of the primary working leg muscles ... for 8-12 minutes; massage of the segmental areas of the back and torso for 3-5 minutes." Pace groups: hot pine-bath hydromassage "for 3-5 minutes, needle or cold shower for 8-13 minutes," and brisk pre-start leg massage "for 8-12 minutes" among other steps (PDF 463, numbers checked against the page image).
733	    20	- *Outdoor track competitions*: "15-20 minutes before," brisk massage "for 8-10 minutes" with heating embrocations; after, "a warm pine or sea bath for 10-15 minutes, a warm rain-type shower and restorative massage for 30 minutes" (PDF 464 / p.453, checked against the page image).
734	    21	- *Immediate pre-competitive preparation* is "The most concentrated period of use of physical means," with "the entire arsenal," including progressive relaxation, self-hypnosis, guided imagery and autogenics (PDF 464).
735	    22	Table 8.11 gives a pre-competition "'shock' microcycle," read cell by cell from the page image (PDF 464 / p.453), as type/magnitude then restorative measures. AM: Day 1 aerobic/medium, warm salt bath; Day 2 aerobic/medium, localised hand massage; Day 3 aerobic/light, contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage; Day 4 aerobic/light, sauna and local hand massage; Day 5 aerobic/medium, localised hand massage; Day 6 aerobic/medium, warm salt bath; Day 7 aerobic/medium, contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage. PM: Day 1 anaerobic/medium, warm pine bath and local hand massage with restorative balsams; Day 2 speed/heavy, indifferent equivalent bath, hydromassage, warm rain shower; Day 3 anaerobic/heavy, hot pine bath, Charcot shower (stream), local massage of the working muscles with restorative balsams; Day 4 blank; Day 5 complex/heavy, warm pine bath, hydromassage, warm rain-type shower; Day 6 complex/medium, warm equivalent bath, hot stream shower, local massage of working muscles; Day 7 complex/heavy, sauna, whole-body restorative massage, contrast procedures.
736	    23	
737	    24	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale: "Because the same restorative means diminish their effectiveness when they are used over prolonged periods, the restorative means were alternated, regarding both content and volume, depending on the stage of the annual cycle" (PDF 463). Throughout, "Special local muscle relaxing and range of movement activities formed an integral component of all training sessions to minimise drops in training effectiveness due to negative acute after-effects of any exercises" (PDF 464). Inference: the table pairs the heaviest restoration (sauna and whole-body massage, hot pine bath with Charcot shower) with the heavy PM sessions and keeps the AM aerobic sessions on light means.
738	    25	
739	    26	**When to apply** — As a template for writing restoration into a periodised plan: basic means in high-volume base stages, on-going means as specialisation rises, operative (stimulating) means before competition, and a day-by-day restorative column in the microcycle table.
740	    27	
741	    28	**When NOT to apply** — "Successfully" is the book's word; no performance or injury data are given, so `untested`. The programme is for elite track cyclists with full-time medical and therapy staff; many means (ionised air, light therapy, barometric techniques) are not available or supported in most programmes. Inference: the AM/PM pattern assumes two sessions a day; a one-session team day cannot copy it directly. The Day 4 PM cell is blank in the table, with no explanation.
742	    29	
743	    30	**Example** — Day 3 of the shock microcycle: an AM aerobic/light session with a contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage, then a PM anaerobic/heavy session followed by a hot pine bath, Charcot shower and local massage of the working muscles with restorative balsams (Table 8.11, PDF 464 / p.453).
744	    31	
745	    32	**Related** — [[principle--periodise-restoration-in-complexes-not-at-random]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]], [[heuristic--shock-microcycle-limits]], [[framework--matveyev-microcycle-and-mesocycle-types-and-sequences]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]]

759	    13	
760	    14	# Massage as a Prescribed Means: Its Methods, Variables, Sport Roles and Contraindications (Tables 8.8-8.10)
761	    15	
762	    16	**What it is** — "The popularity of massage deems that further details of its different methods be given" (PDF 459 / p.448). From the page images:
763	    17	- *Methods* (Table 8.8, PDF 459 / p.448), 20 cells in two columns: effleurage (long, smooth stroking); frottage (rubbing); petrissage (kneading); friction (deep kneading); tapotement (percussion); vibration (trembling, shaking); nerve stroking (light stroking); "Rolling, wringing, jostling"; squeezing; drilling; pressing (sustained or oscillatory); slapping; hacking; "Lifting, pulling"; "Clapping, cupping"; deep transverse friction; Therapeutic Touch; cryokinetics; barotherapy; electrostimulation.
764	    18	- *Variables* (Table 8.9, PDF 459), 20: means, methods, apparatus, hand or other massaging contact, depth, frequency, pressure, lubricant, positioning, sequence; duration, tempo, environment, psychological state, direction, rest intervals, therapist personal features, client personal features, variation, "Ethics, privacy, respect." The text adds contact points (palms, finger tips, knuckles, knife-edge of hand, thumb, fist, elbow, feet) and modes of movement (linear, circular, spiral, transverse or longitudinal to the muscle, pulsating, vibrating, squeezing, twisting, pinching, lifting, pressing).
765	    19	- *Roles in sports preparation*, "as described by many Russian experts": "Warming; Loosening; Pre-start relaxation; Pre-start stimulation; Mobilisation; Restoration during and after workouts or competitions" (PDF 459-460 / p.448-449).
766	    20	- *Contraindications* (Table 8.10, PDF 460 / p.449), 18: broken or bleeding tissue; inflamed, bruised, swollen tissue; strains, sprains, tissue rupture; varicose veins; painful, hypersensitive regions; phlebitis; thrombosis; swellings, lumps, moles, warts; fractures; arthritis with inflammation; stomach area during pregnancy; stomach area during nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, gastric upset; haemorrhaged tissue; jaundice; "Thigh, hip, chest, gluteal massage during menstruation"; dermatitis, urticaria or any skin irritation or allergy; contagious conditions; malignant tissue.
767	    21	
768	    22	**Why it works** — The authors treat massage "like any other form of therapy," which "can pose certain risks" (PDF 460). Inference: separating method (what is done) from variables (how it is dosed) and role (why) is what lets two sessions called "massage" be compared at all; without it, the claims and counter-claims the authors describe cannot be tested.
769	    23	
770	    24	**When to apply** — When a massage is part of a warm-up, a pre-start routine or restoration, state its role first (warming, loosening, relaxing, stimulating, mobilising, restoring), then pick method and variables to fit, then screen against the contraindications. The authors also require the practitioner to "be aware of any personal limitations" and call on someone "more qualified in certain fields" (PDF 460).
771	    25	
772	    26	**When NOT to apply** — The tables are lists without evidence of effect for each method; inclusion of Therapeutic Touch and barotherapy is not support for them. The contraindication list "refers specifically to massage which makes definite contact with the body" and "only to physical contra-indications; there are also several good psychological or ethical reasons why massage might be contraindicated" (PDF 460). Some entries reflect the book's era and are not current clinical guidance as written (for example, the menstruation item). Inference: in a university setting, contraindication screening sits with licensed medical staff.
773	    27	
774	    28	**Example** — The six roles applied to a pre-race routine in the book's own cycling case: "brisk pre-start massage of the primary working leg muscles (using stroking, rubbing, kneading, shaking) for 8-12 minutes" is the "pre-start stimulation" role (PDF 463 / p.452; see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]).
775	    29	
776	    30	**Related** — [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]], [[claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it]], [[heuristic--choose-massage-technique-by-goal]], [[framework--restoration-prescription-checklist-and-means-versus-methods]], [[heuristic--rotate-restorative-means-and-rest-local-procedures]] (the complementarity effect)

790	    13	
791	    14	# Massage Effects Depend on the Athlete's Initial State and the Technique Used, Not Only Placebo (Birukov and Pelsahov, Fig 8.5)
792	    15	
793	    16	**What it is** — To "correct" the "tendency to dismiss the effects of many restorative means as placebo or psychological in origin," the authors cite Birukov & Pelsahov (1979), who found that massage "indeed causes effects which are not simply placebo or circulatory in nature," with "different effects of massage on the central and peripheral systems, as well as differences in the effects produced by each different type of massage (Fig 8.5)" (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page image). Four findings:
794	    17	1. "Massage does not have an identical effect on the central and peripheral systems of the body. The condition of the peripheral systems changes in the same direction, while the functional state of the brain changes over a much wider range, depending on the initial levels existing before the massage."
795	    18	2. "Individual massage methods change the condition of the separate subsystems of the body in different ways. The influence of individual massage techniques depends largely on the initial functional condition before the application of massage."
796	    19	3. "Massage generally has a favourable influence on all subsystems of the body, optimising their state by increasing or decreasing the level of activation of the cortex and sub-cortical systems of the brain."
797	    20	4. "When using massage as a method of restructuring and restoring, it is necessary to differentiate the approach by taking into consideration the initial level of excitation," using measures "such as simple reaction time, skin impedance, dynamometry and tonometry" (PDF 465).
798	    21	Fig 8.5 (PDF 466 / p.455, read from the figure) plots four indices (reaction time, axis about 149-157; skin resistance in kilo-ohm, about 30-110; dynamometer force in kgf, about 40-60; tonometer reading in mm, about 70-90) before and after four techniques (stroking; squeezing; kneading; slapping, clapping, percussion), with three lines each: athletes with maximum, mean and minimum initial values. The caption calls these "three groups of athletes, distinguished by their initial levels."
799	    22	
800	    23	**Why it works** — The authors' reading (finding 3) is that massage "optimises" state rather than pushing it one way. Inference, from the figure: in most panels the "max" line falls and the "min" line rises, so groups converge toward the middle; for example skin resistance and reaction time fall in the max group and rise in the min group under all four techniques. The figure is not uniform: under stroking, tonometer readings fall in all three groups and dynamometer force stays roughly flat (max, mean) or falls (min), while under squeezing, kneading and percussion both indices rise in all three groups.
801	    24	
802	    25	**When to apply** — Before choosing a massage technique for restoration, measure or at least judge the athlete's starting state (aroused or flat), since the same technique can move different athletes in different directions. The authors' indicators are reaction time, skin impedance, grip dynamometry and tonometry (PDF 465).
803	    26	
804	    27	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample size, statistics or control condition, and the figure's reaction-time axis has no unit. The convergence pattern is this entry's reading of the figure, not a statement in the text. Inference: grouping athletes by their extreme initial values invites regression to the mean, which would make max groups fall and min groups rise even without any treatment; the book does not address this.
805	    28	
806	    29	**Example** — Finding 4 in practice: the authors tie the choice of massage approach to "the initial level of excitation," measured by "simple reaction time, skin impedance, dynamometry and tonometry" (PDF 465 / p.454).
807	    30	
808	    31	**Related** — [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[heuristic--choose-massage-technique-by-goal]], [[case-study--makarova-stupnitsky-weekly-four-group-restoration-triage-fig-8-4]], [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]]

823	    14	# Manual Massage Raises Muscle Blood Flow by Dilating Small Arteries; Mechanical Vibromassage at 35-100 Hz Lowers It
824	    15	
825	    16	**What it is** — Two Russian findings the authors cite. Dubrovsky (1982), using "the injection of radioactive Xenon markers into the blood," found that "sports massage dilates the peripheral blood vessels, speeds up venous and muscle blood flow, and causes a small, but significant, increase in the oxygen saturation of arterial blood"; concurrent myotonometer readings "revealed a decrease in muscle tone," which Dubrovsky attributed to the enhanced blood flow (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page image). Burovykh et al (1976): "mechanical vibromassage (35-100 Hz) causes an acute decrease in blood circulation, associated with the vasoconstrictive effect of vibration," and "the increase in muscle blood supply after manual massage is due primarily to dilation of the lumen of the small arterial vessels, rather than the popularly believed concept of venous drainage." The same work linked blood-flow gains to "the tissue warming effects of some forms of massage" and showed "a decrease in muscle temperature (0.5-1.0 deg C) due to vibromassage" (PDF 465, numbers checked against the page image).
826	    17	
827	    18	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: manual massage dilates small arteries and warms tissue; high-frequency vibration constricts vessels and cools muscle (PDF 465). The authors' implication: "deep manual massage is more effective for enhancing blood flow and relaxation than higher frequency vibromassage, which should be used for the reflexogenic application of stimulating the neuromuscular system." With an adjustable vibromassager, "lower frequencies (10-15 Hz) can be used to promote general restoration, blood flow, muscle relaxation and decreased arterial pressure, provided that care is taken not to apply it over nervous plexuses or prominent bony areas" (PDF 465). They add that Dubrovsky's tone finding "emphasizes that mild active restoration offers some definite advantages over strictly passive methods on their own" (PDF 465).
828	    19	
829	    20	**When to apply** — When a percussion or vibration device is used for "recovery," check its frequency and the aim: for blood flow and relaxation, the book favours deep manual work or low-frequency (10-15 Hz) vibration; for stimulation before effort, higher-frequency vibration. Eric's review: "recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: by these findings a high-frequency percussion gun is a stimulation tool more than a blood-flow tool.
830	    21	
831	    22	**When NOT to apply** — The studies are cited, not described: no sample sizes, protocols or effect sizes beyond the 0.5-1.0 deg C temperature drop and the frequency bands. The 35-100 Hz finding is for 1970s mechanical vibromassagers; Inference: modern percussion devices differ in amplitude and contact, so the result transfers only by analogy. The 10-15 Hz recommendation is the authors' inference from these studies, not a tested protocol. The Dubrovsky sentence is printed ungrammatically ("conclude that decrease in muscle tone caused by enhanced blood flow"), so the direction of cause is the reading most consistent with the context.
832	    23	
833	    24	**Example** — Burovykh et al's contrast: manual massage raised muscle blood supply through arterial dilation, while vibromassage at 35-100 Hz cut circulation and lowered muscle temperature by 0.5-1.0 deg C (PDF 465 / p.454).
834	    25	
835	    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--choose-massage-technique-by-goal]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (low-frequency vibromassage in runners), [[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]

850	    14	# Choose the Massage Technique by Goal: Proximal First and Deep for Blood Flow, Percussion Only for Stimulation, Reflexive Points for Fast Central Recovery
851	    15	
852	    16	**What it is** — "Other findings emerging from this and related work" (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page images of PDF 465-466):
853	    17	- "Massage of the proximal, larger muscles before the distal muscles, if blood circulation is to be maximally encouraged."
854	    18	- "Deeper massage techniques (such as kneading and squeezing) should be used preferentially if one wishes to stimulate blood flow and muscle metabolism."
855	    19	- "Percussive massage methods (such as chopping, tapping and slapping) stimulate the nervous system, raise venous pressure and diminish blood microcirculation, so they should not be used for relaxation or general restoration."
856	    20	- "Reflexive massage (e.g. acupressure point, trigger point) techniques often produce a more marked and quicker recovery after training sessions, so that it may be unnecessary to rely solely on more conventional means, especially if restoration of the central nervous system is desired (Peshkov, 1981)" (PDF 466 / p.455).
857	    21	
858	    22	**Why it works** — The rules follow the blood-flow findings: deep manual work dilates small arteries, while percussion and high-frequency vibration constrict vessels and stimulate the nervous system (PDF 465; see [[claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it]]). Inference: working proximal muscles first clears the larger venous path before distal tissue is pushed into it; the book states the rule, not this reason.
859	    23	
860	    24	**When to apply** — Post-session restoration: deep techniques, proximal before distal, no percussion. Pre-start stimulation: percussion and brisk techniques are appropriate, which matches the cycling team's "brisk pre-start massage" (see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]). When the aim is central nervous recovery, the authors point to reflexive point techniques.
861	    25	
862	    26	**When NOT to apply** — Except for Peshkov (1981), the rules are attributed to "this and related work" without data; `untested`. The reflexive-massage claim is hedged by its own wording ("often," "may be unnecessary"). All four rules sit under the contraindications in Table 8.10 (see [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]]).
863	    27	
864	    28	**Example** — Inference, applied: after a lower-body strength session, kneading and squeezing of the glutes and thighs before the calves; the same athlete before a sprint session gets brisk tapping and rubbing of the legs instead.
865	    29	
866	    30	**Related** — [[claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it]], [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]

879	    12	---
880	    13	
881	    14	# Eighteen Propositions on Sport Science and Stress Management
882	    15	
883	    16	**What it is** — The last sub-section of 8.6, "Sports Science and Stress Management," sits at the top of PDF 467 / p.456, above the 8.7 heading. The authors: "all training is a form of stressing the body in an optimal manner," and training principles "are very useful in helping one cope with physical and mental stress both in and away from the competitive arena." They then give a list "assembled largely from previous chapters of this text" (PDF 467, checked against the page image). Grouped here by theme (the grouping is this entry's; numbers are the book's):
884	    17	- *Belief and delivery* (1-4): "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it"; techniques obtained "at high cost in terms of effort, cash or commitment," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or appealing to "the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user" are more likely to succeed.
885	    18	- *Individual and dynamic* (5-6, 14): "No technique is universally superior to another: a given technique is better for a given individual in a given situation at a given time"; stress "is not static, but a dynamic physiological and psychological process"; it "may be managed by use of physiological or psychological techniques."
886	    19	- *Dose and adaptation* (8-12): optimise, "though not necessarily avoid or diminish stress"; but "The concept of stress optimisation is not always accurate: high performance may occur with altered states of consciousness when stress levels are very high or very low"; exposure "may produce either adaptation or sensitisation"; the first response may be "flight or fight, but also freezing ... which may be the most damaging effect of stress"; planned exposure to manageable stress "may enable one to cope with higher levels of stress."
887	    20	- *Perception and movement* (13, 15): understanding "kinaesthetic and motor" processes "is invaluable"; "Our perception or interpretation of stress or pain may be more powerful than the stress, pain or stimulus itself."
888	    21	- *Mind models* (7, 16-18): the subconscious or "superconscious"; Jung's four functions (sensation, intuition, thinking, feeling); brain regions beyond the left-right cortex; and access to "a vast seldom-tapped source of energy via specific altered states of consciousness."
889	    22	
890	    23	**Why it works** — The authors' frame is that stress tolerance is trainable like any other quality: "*Superadaptation* (supercompensation) or *innoculation* against specific stresses is possible by exposing yourself to properly structured doses of manageable stress" (PDF 467). Inference: items 8-12 carry the training logic; items 1-4 and 15 carry the psychological logic that the placebo discussion earlier in 8.6 develops.
891	    24	
892	    25	**When to apply** — As a set of prompts when an athlete's response to stress (competition, injury, life events) is the problem: is the response adaptation or sensitisation (10), freezing rather than fight-or-flight (11), driven by perception more than the stressor (15)? Inference: items 5 and 10 argue for individual, revised plans rather than a fixed team routine.
893	    26	
894	    27	**When NOT to apply** — The list cites no studies; items 7 and 16-18 (the "superconscious," Jung's types, a "seldom-tapped source of energy") are speculative and outside sport science as practised. Item 1 ("any technique will work ... if you believe in it") overstates the placebo point the authors make more carefully on PDF 455-456, and item 9 qualifies item 8 on the same page. Treat the list as the authors' views, not findings.
895	    28	
896	    29	**Example** — Item 15 in the authors' own words: "alteration of our perceptions and thoughts may manage the stress effectively," and "our perception or assessment of the attractiveness or repulsiveness of the stressor can alter our belief that the stressor can be managed" (PDF 467 / p.456).
897	    30	
898	    31	**Related** — [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]], [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]], [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Talyshev: Sauna Plus Hydrotherapy Right After a Workout Helped That Day but Hurt the Next; 6-9 Hours Later It Produced Supercompensation
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Talyshev (1977) "conducted research on a large group of highly qualified athletes who followed a standardised training programme. Following a workout, the athletes took a sauna in combination with hydrotherapy - in one case directly after the workout; in the other cases, 3, 6, and 9 hours later, accompanied by a large battery of physiological tests" (PDF 462 / p.451, checked against the page image). Results as reported:
    17	- No baths or hydrotherapy: work capacity "dropped sharply immediately after the workout," and "noticeable recovery commenced on the following day."
    18	- Immediately after: "a marked increase in work capacity immediately following the therapy and 3 hours later. However, this increase slowed down, and work capacity did not recover and even fell below its initial level on the following day."
    19	- At 3 hours: "a pronounced increase in work capacity 6 hours after the therapy (9 hours after the workout). Work capacity returned to its initial level on the following day."
    20	- At 6, "and especially 9 hours": "work capacity not only recovered on the following day, but there was significant increase (supercompensation)" (PDF 462 / p.451).
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The setup in the book: "The highest intensity and rate of recovery is observed immediately upon cessation of exercise, after which it diminishes gradually (Talyshev, 1977). Logically, *it is more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down*" (PDF 462, italics in the original). The book frames recovery in three phases (Zalessky, 1979): "On-going recovery" during activity; "Rapid recovery" immediately after, "leading to removal of metabolic by-products and replenishment of depleted energy resources"; and "Delayed recovery, which surpasses the initial level if training loads are not excessive" (PDF 455 / p.444). Inference: an intervention during the rapid phase adds little to a process already running fast and may cut short the signal; one in the delayed phase supports the process when it slows.
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — As evidence for timing heat and water therapies by the next performance demand, not by habit (see [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]]).
    25	
    26	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample size, no measure of "work capacity," no statistics and no control for the order of conditions; "large group of highly qualified athletes" is all that is said. The result is for sauna plus hydrotherapy; it says nothing on its own about massage, cold or compression. The "no therapy" condition is described only qualitatively, so the supercompensation at 6-9 hours is not compared numerically with it.
    27

    14	# Time Restoration to When Work Capacity Is Next Needed: Immediately for the Same Day, 6-9 Hours Later for Tomorrow; Whole-Body After General Work, Local After Local
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Talyshev's (1977) conclusion from his timing study: "work capacity and its magnitude depend strongly on the time at which the restorative methods are applied. When an immediate effect is necessary, namely when the greatest work capacity recovery after a short span of time is needed (e.g. between morning and afternoon workouts), it is advisable to employ restorative methods immediately after workouts or morning starts. If, however, a high work capacity is required on the following day, then it is better to employ recovery methods 6-9 hours after the workout or competition. If the workout or competition ends late in the evening, it is preferable to start recovery procedures in the morning, shortly after awakening" (PDF 462 / p.451, checked against the page image). A second rule from "Related work": "it is best to employ full-body recovery methods (e.g. sauna, hydrotherapy, general massage) after large volume of general training work. In contrast, local methods (e.g. pressure methods, local manual or vibrational massage, local heating) are preferable following the execution of work which strongly stresses specific muscle groups" (PDF 462).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The basis is the study (see [[case-study--talyshev-sauna-and-hydrotherapy-timing-0-3-6-9-hours]]): immediate therapy raised work capacity for a few hours but left it below baseline the next day, while therapy at 6-9 hours produced next-day supercompensation (PDF 462). The authors' framing: recovery is fastest straight after exercise, so it is "more advisable to accelerate recovery processes when their natural rate is slowing down" (PDF 462).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Two-a-days and tournaments: restoration straight after the first session. Normal training days with the next key session tomorrow: restoration in the evening, roughly 6-9 hours after training, or the next morning if training ended late. Choose whole-body means after high-volume general work and local means after work that hammered one muscle group. Eric's review: "Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)). Inference: the baseline schedules recovery by day; the book's rule would add a time-of-day decision inside the day.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The data come from one study of sauna with hydrotherapy in highly qualified athletes, reported without numbers (see the case study). The whole-body versus local rule is cited only as "Related work," and the authors concede it is "still fairly general and the question remains as to how does the dosage of a specific recovery method relates to the severity of the training load" (PDF 462). Inference: in a game week where the priority is the game, not adaptation, the immediate option may be right even for next-day readiness; the book does not address that trade-off.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' own case for immediate use: "between morning and afternoon workouts" (PDF 462 / p.451). Their case for delay: a workout or competition ending late in the evening, with recovery started "in the morning, shortly after awakening."

    14	# Judge a Restoration Method by Performance and Injuries, Not Client Feeling, and Test It Under Sport-Typical Loads
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two rules for evaluating restoration. First: "Client feeling and appreciation are not enough; in sports restoration, the basic indicators are improved performance and fewer injuries." The reader should "experiment with variations, to keep records and to devise recipes which consistently yield successful results" (PDF 460 / p.449, checked against the page image). Second, from Talyshev (1977): because "it is very difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of specific recovery method," it "is more advisable to test the effectiveness of a specific recovery method by using test loads that approximate most closely the natural training conditions, by using loads in sports exercises that are typically encountered in a given sport" (PDF 460-461 / p.449-450, checked against the page images).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for caution: "if certain recovery methods are employed after a workout, then the positive after-effects (or training effect) stimulated by the workout tend to be negated," so "the unskilled use of recovery methods can markedly increase the amount of training work and yet not provide a corresponding training effect" (PDF 460 / p.449). Inference: an athlete can feel better and train more while adapting less, so feeling and session volume are the wrong outcome measures; performance and injury rate capture the net effect.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a modality is adopted or kept, write down what outcome it is meant to change, track performance and injuries across its use, and test it with the sport's own loads (for example a repeated-sprint or practice-like session) rather than a lab task. Eric's review: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 89, Explicit). Inference: the same distrust of self-report that ended the surveys applies to "this feels good" as evidence for a recovery tool.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Performance and injury rate are slow, noisy outcomes; Inference: with a small group they cannot separate one modality's effect within a season, so the rule supports keeping records over time rather than quick verdicts. The book gives no example of a method that was dropped under this rule. Feeling still matters for adherence and is part of the placebo effect the authors elsewhere call useful (see [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors' framing of Russian work: "systematic use of recovery methods makes it possible to significantly and sometimes rapidly increase the volume and intensity of training while simultaneously decreasing the incidence of musculoskeletal injuries" (PDF 460 / p.449), which names the two outcomes, training capacity and injuries, they want restoration judged on.
    25

    14	# Periodise Restoration in Complexes Tied to the Training Stage; Do Not Apply It at Random or Because the Athlete Feels Tired
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under "Complexes and Periodisation in Restoration": "The tendency to apply restorative means and methods largely at random, depending on one's preferences and training, should be avoided, since different processes or body components (nervous, muscular, ligamentous, metabolic, psychological, cardiovascular etc.) fatigue, recover and adapt at different rates and to different degrees, depending on the nature of the loading and the athlete. The value of combining, complexing and periodising training loads according to individualised programmes has achieved a high degree of acceptance, but the value of a similar approach in restoration often tends to be ignored" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image). Because manual methods cannot be given volumes and intensities like training loads, "one more frequently refers to the use of restorative complexes or of periodised training programmes which incorporate restorative procedures" (PDF 463). The failure the authors name: "inappropriate timing can delay or even reverse recovery after training, yet many well-meaning therapists quite casually employ massage, spinal manipulation, electrostimulation, hydrotherapy and other common methods simply because the athlete feels 'tired', sore, stressed or unmotivated" (PDF 463).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is differential recovery: tissues and systems recover at different rates, so one routine applied at random will be early for some and late for others (PDF 463). Inference: grouping means into complexes matched to a training stage lets the restoration target the system that the stage loads most.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When writing the annual plan, write the restoration plan alongside it: which complex in which stage, and what changes as the stage changes. Treat "the athlete feels tired" as a cue to check the plan, not as an order for a treatment.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — No outcome data here; the authors defer "A more thorough exposition" to Siff & Yessis (1992) and give one example (PDF 463). Inference: this principle concerns planned restoration; it does not forbid responding to an injury or an acute medical need, which the book places under rehabilitation.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The book's worked example is the Soviet track cycling team's five-year programme, where the restorative means were "closely linked to the objectives of the individual stages of training" (PDF 463 / p.452; see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]], [[principle--restoration-is-part-of-training-and-distinct-from-rehabilitation]], [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[browns-strength-and-conditioning-2008--myslinski/heuristic--restoration-emphasis-rises-as-the-off-season-advances]]
