    14	# Soviet Track Cycling: Three Groups of Restorative Means Matched to Each Training Stage, and a Shock Microcycle With Restoration Twice a Day (Table 8.11)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "The Soviet track cycling team, for a period of 5 years, successfully used this type of programme of restoration, (Goletz & Osadchy, 1986)," with three groups of means: "Group 1 (Basic means) for rapidly eliminating the fatigue following a training session"; "Group 2 (On-going means) for restoring the individual components of athletic preparedness to elevate the work capacity of these components during subsequent training sessions"; "Group 3 (Operative means) for stimulating work capacity directly before or during a workout or competition" (PDF 463 / p.452, checked against the page image). By stage:
    17	- *General base-building*: "only *basic* type restorative means," because the stage has "concentrated, high-volume workloads." At the end of the microcycle, before a rest day: a hydro session or short gentle swim, restorative massage, warm baths with essences (pine, eucalyptus, sea salt), and a hot-cold contrast bath or shower (PDF 463).
    18	- *Progressing training*: basic and on-going means per the microcycle plan, adding localised manual massage, showers and light therapy; at microcycle end, hydro procedures with electrotherapy, electromagnetic fields, ultrasound and barometric techniques (PDF 463).
    19	- *Winter indoor competitions*: more "non-relaxing *operative* means." Sprint and heat groups: "brisk pre-start massage of the primary working leg muscles ... for 8-12 minutes; massage of the segmental areas of the back and torso for 3-5 minutes." Pace groups: hot pine-bath hydromassage "for 3-5 minutes, needle or cold shower for 8-13 minutes," and brisk pre-start leg massage "for 8-12 minutes" among other steps (PDF 463, numbers checked against the page image).
    20	- *Outdoor track competitions*: "15-20 minutes before," brisk massage "for 8-10 minutes" with heating embrocations; after, "a warm pine or sea bath for 10-15 minutes, a warm rain-type shower and restorative massage for 30 minutes" (PDF 464 / p.453, checked against the page image).
    21	- *Immediate pre-competitive preparation* is "The most concentrated period of use of physical means," with "the entire arsenal," including progressive relaxation, self-hypnosis, guided imagery and autogenics (PDF 464).
    22	Table 8.11 gives a pre-competition "'shock' microcycle," read cell by cell from the page image (PDF 464 / p.453), as type/magnitude then restorative measures. AM: Day 1 aerobic/medium, warm salt bath; Day 2 aerobic/medium, localised hand massage; Day 3 aerobic/light, contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage; Day 4 aerobic/light, sauna and local hand massage; Day 5 aerobic/medium, localised hand massage; Day 6 aerobic/medium, warm salt bath; Day 7 aerobic/medium, contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage. PM: Day 1 anaerobic/medium, warm pine bath and local hand massage with restorative balsams; Day 2 speed/heavy, indifferent equivalent bath, hydromassage, warm rain shower; Day 3 anaerobic/heavy, hot pine bath, Charcot shower (stream), local massage of the working muscles with restorative balsams; Day 4 blank; Day 5 complex/heavy, warm pine bath, hydromassage, warm rain-type shower; Day 6 complex/medium, warm equivalent bath, hot stream shower, local massage of working muscles; Day 7 complex/heavy, sauna, whole-body restorative massage, contrast procedures.
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale: "Because the same restorative means diminish their effectiveness when they are used over prolonged periods, the restorative means were alternated, regarding both content and volume, depending on the stage of the annual cycle" (PDF 463). Throughout, "Special local muscle relaxing and range of movement activities formed an integral component of all training sessions to minimise drops in training effectiveness due to negative acute after-effects of any exercises" (PDF 464). Inference: the table pairs the heaviest restoration (sauna and whole-body massage, hot pine bath with Charcot shower) with the heavy PM sessions and keeps the AM aerobic sessions on light means.
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — As a template for writing restoration into a periodised plan: basic means in high-volume base stages, on-going means as specialisation rises, operative (stimulating) means before competition, and a day-by-day restorative column in the microcycle table.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — "Successfully" is the book's word; no performance or injury data are given, so `untested`. The programme is for elite track cyclists with full-time medical and therapy staff; many means (ionised air, light therapy, barometric techniques) are not available or supported in most programmes. Inference: the AM/PM pattern assumes two sessions a day; a one-session team day cannot copy it directly. The Day 4 PM cell is blank in the table, with no explanation.
    29	
    30	**Example** — Day 3 of the shock microcycle: an AM aerobic/light session with a contrast rain-type shower and segmental massage, then a PM anaerobic/heavy session followed by a hot pine bath, Charcot shower and local massage of the working muscles with restorative balsams (Table 8.11, PDF 464 / p.453).

    14	# Massage as a Prescribed Means: Its Methods, Variables, Sport Roles and Contraindications (Tables 8.8-8.10)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "The popularity of massage deems that further details of its different methods be given" (PDF 459 / p.448). From the page images:
    17	- *Methods* (Table 8.8, PDF 459 / p.448), 20 cells in two columns: effleurage (long, smooth stroking); frottage (rubbing); petrissage (kneading); friction (deep kneading); tapotement (percussion); vibration (trembling, shaking); nerve stroking (light stroking); "Rolling, wringing, jostling"; squeezing; drilling; pressing (sustained or oscillatory); slapping; hacking; "Lifting, pulling"; "Clapping, cupping"; deep transverse friction; Therapeutic Touch; cryokinetics; barotherapy; electrostimulation.
    18	- *Variables* (Table 8.9, PDF 459), 20: means, methods, apparatus, hand or other massaging contact, depth, frequency, pressure, lubricant, positioning, sequence; duration, tempo, environment, psychological state, direction, rest intervals, therapist personal features, client personal features, variation, "Ethics, privacy, respect." The text adds contact points (palms, finger tips, knuckles, knife-edge of hand, thumb, fist, elbow, feet) and modes of movement (linear, circular, spiral, transverse or longitudinal to the muscle, pulsating, vibrating, squeezing, twisting, pinching, lifting, pressing).
    19	- *Roles in sports preparation*, "as described by many Russian experts": "Warming; Loosening; Pre-start relaxation; Pre-start stimulation; Mobilisation; Restoration during and after workouts or competitions" (PDF 459-460 / p.448-449).
    20	- *Contraindications* (Table 8.10, PDF 460 / p.449), 18: broken or bleeding tissue; inflamed, bruised, swollen tissue; strains, sprains, tissue rupture; varicose veins; painful, hypersensitive regions; phlebitis; thrombosis; swellings, lumps, moles, warts; fractures; arthritis with inflammation; stomach area during pregnancy; stomach area during nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, gastric upset; haemorrhaged tissue; jaundice; "Thigh, hip, chest, gluteal massage during menstruation"; dermatitis, urticaria or any skin irritation or allergy; contagious conditions; malignant tissue.
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The authors treat massage "like any other form of therapy," which "can pose certain risks" (PDF 460). Inference: separating method (what is done) from variables (how it is dosed) and role (why) is what lets two sessions called "massage" be compared at all; without it, the claims and counter-claims the authors describe cannot be tested.
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — When a massage is part of a warm-up, a pre-start routine or restoration, state its role first (warming, loosening, relaxing, stimulating, mobilising, restoring), then pick method and variables to fit, then screen against the contraindications. The authors also require the practitioner to "be aware of any personal limitations" and call on someone "more qualified in certain fields" (PDF 460).
    25

    18	2. "Individual massage methods change the condition of the separate subsystems of the body in different ways. The influence of individual massage techniques depends largely on the initial functional condition before the application of massage."
    19	3. "Massage generally has a favourable influence on all subsystems of the body, optimising their state by increasing or decreasing the level of activation of the cortex and sub-cortical systems of the brain."

    14	# Manual Massage Raises Muscle Blood Flow by Dilating Small Arteries; Mechanical Vibromassage at 35-100 Hz Lowers It
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two Russian findings the authors cite. Dubrovsky (1982), using "the injection of radioactive Xenon markers into the blood," found that "sports massage dilates the peripheral blood vessels, speeds up venous and muscle blood flow, and causes a small, but significant, increase in the oxygen saturation of arterial blood"; concurrent myotonometer readings "revealed a decrease in muscle tone," which Dubrovsky attributed to the enhanced blood flow (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page image). Burovykh et al (1976): "mechanical vibromassage (35-100 Hz) causes an acute decrease in blood circulation, associated with the vasoconstrictive effect of vibration," and "the increase in muscle blood supply after manual massage is due primarily to dilation of the lumen of the small arterial vessels, rather than the popularly believed concept of venous drainage." The same work linked blood-flow gains to "the tissue warming effects of some forms of massage" and showed "a decrease in muscle temperature (0.5-1.0 deg C) due to vibromassage" (PDF 465, numbers checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism: manual massage dilates small arteries and warms tissue; high-frequency vibration constricts vessels and cools muscle (PDF 465). The authors' implication: "deep manual massage is more effective for enhancing blood flow and relaxation than higher frequency vibromassage, which should be used for the reflexogenic application of stimulating the neuromuscular system." With an adjustable vibromassager, "lower frequencies (10-15 Hz) can be used to promote general restoration, blood flow, muscle relaxation and decreased arterial pressure, provided that care is taken not to apply it over nervous plexuses or prominent bony areas" (PDF 465). They add that Dubrovsky's tone finding "emphasizes that mild active restoration offers some definite advantages over strictly passive methods on their own" (PDF 465).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a percussion or vibration device is used for "recovery," check its frequency and the aim: for blood flow and relaxation, the book favours deep manual work or low-frequency (10-15 Hz) vibration; for stimulation before effort, higher-frequency vibration. Eric's review: "recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: by these findings a high-frequency percussion gun is a stimulation tool more than a blood-flow tool.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The studies are cited, not described: no sample sizes, protocols or effect sizes beyond the 0.5-1.0 deg C temperature drop and the frequency bands. The 35-100 Hz finding is for 1970s mechanical vibromassagers; Inference: modern percussion devices differ in amplitude and contact, so the result transfers only by analogy. The 10-15 Hz recommendation is the authors' inference from these studies, not a tested protocol. The Dubrovsky sentence is printed ungrammatically ("conclude that decrease in muscle tone caused by enhanced blood flow"), so the direction of cause is the reading most consistent with the context.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Burovykh et al's contrast: manual massage raised muscle blood supply through arterial dilation, while vibromassage at 35-100 Hz cut circulation and lowered muscle temperature by 0.5-1.0 deg C (PDF 465 / p.454).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[heuristic--choose-massage-technique-by-goal]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (low-frequency vibromassage in runners), [[research-papers/dupuy-2018-an-evidence-based-approach-for-choosing-post-exercise-recovery-techniques-to-reduce-marker]]

    13	
    14	# Choose the Massage Technique by Goal: Proximal First and Deep for Blood Flow, Percussion Only for Stimulation, Reflexive Points for Fast Central Recovery
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "Other findings emerging from this and related work" (PDF 465 / p.454, checked against the page images of PDF 465-466):
    17	- "Massage of the proximal, larger muscles before the distal muscles, if blood circulation is to be maximally encouraged."
    18	- "Deeper massage techniques (such as kneading and squeezing) should be used preferentially if one wishes to stimulate blood flow and muscle metabolism."
    19	- "Percussive massage methods (such as chopping, tapping and slapping) stimulate the nervous system, raise venous pressure and diminish blood microcirculation, so they should not be used for relaxation or general restoration."
    20	- "Reflexive massage (e.g. acupressure point, trigger point) techniques often produce a more marked and quicker recovery after training sessions, so that it may be unnecessary to rely solely on more conventional means, especially if restoration of the central nervous system is desired (Peshkov, 1981)" (PDF 466 / p.455).
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The rules follow the blood-flow findings: deep manual work dilates small arteries, while percussion and high-frequency vibration constrict vessels and stimulate the nervous system (PDF 465; see [[claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it]]). Inference: working proximal muscles first clears the larger venous path before distal tissue is pushed into it; the book states the rule, not this reason.
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — Post-session restoration: deep techniques, proximal before distal, no percussion. Pre-start stimulation: percussion and brisk techniques are appropriate, which matches the cycling team's "brisk pre-start massage" (see [[case-study--soviet-track-cycling-restoration-by-stage-and-shock-microcycle-table-8-11]]). When the aim is central nervous recovery, the authors point to reflexive point techniques.
    25	
    26	**When NOT to apply** — Except for Peshkov (1981), the rules are attributed to "this and related work" without data; `untested`. The reflexive-massage claim is hedged by its own wording ("often," "may be unnecessary"). All four rules sit under the contraindications in Table 8.10 (see [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]]).
    27	
    28	**Example** — Inference, applied: after a lower-body strength session, kneading and squeezing of the glutes and thighs before the calves; the same athlete before a sprint session gets brisk tapping and rubbing of the legs instead.
    29	
    30	**Related** — [[claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it]], [[claim--massage-effects-depend-on-initial-state-birukov-pelsahov-fig-8-5]], [[framework--massage-methods-variables-roles-and-contraindications]], [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]

    13	
    14	# Eighteen Propositions on Sport Science and Stress Management
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The last sub-section of 8.6, "Sports Science and Stress Management," sits at the top of PDF 467 / p.456, above the 8.7 heading. The authors: "all training is a form of stressing the body in an optimal manner," and training principles "are very useful in helping one cope with physical and mental stress both in and away from the competitive arena." They then give a list "assembled largely from previous chapters of this text" (PDF 467, checked against the page image). Grouped here by theme (the grouping is this entry's; numbers are the book's):
    17	- *Belief and delivery* (1-4): "Virtually any technique will work, irrespective of scientific validity, if you believe in it"; techniques obtained "at high cost in terms of effort, cash or commitment," taught "in an exciting, emotional or challenging way," or appealing to "the basic beliefs, prejudices and background of the user" are more likely to succeed.
    18	- *Individual and dynamic* (5-6, 14): "No technique is universally superior to another: a given technique is better for a given individual in a given situation at a given time"; stress "is not static, but a dynamic physiological and psychological process"; it "may be managed by use of physiological or psychological techniques."
    19	- *Dose and adaptation* (8-12): optimise, "though not necessarily avoid or diminish stress"; but "The concept of stress optimisation is not always accurate: high performance may occur with altered states of consciousness when stress levels are very high or very low"; exposure "may produce either adaptation or sensitisation"; the first response may be "flight or fight, but also freezing ... which may be the most damaging effect of stress"; planned exposure to manageable stress "may enable one to cope with higher levels of stress."
    20	- *Perception and movement* (13, 15): understanding "kinaesthetic and motor" processes "is invaluable"; "Our perception or interpretation of stress or pain may be more powerful than the stress, pain or stimulus itself."
    21	- *Mind models* (7, 16-18): the subconscious or "superconscious"; Jung's four functions (sensation, intuition, thinking, feeling); brain regions beyond the left-right cortex; and access to "a vast seldom-tapped source of energy via specific altered states of consciousness."
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — The authors' frame is that stress tolerance is trainable like any other quality: "*Superadaptation* (supercompensation) or *innoculation* against specific stresses is possible by exposing yourself to properly structured doses of manageable stress" (PDF 467). Inference: items 8-12 carry the training logic; items 1-4 and 15 carry the psychological logic that the placebo discussion earlier in 8.6 develops.
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — As a set of prompts when an athlete's response to stress (competition, injury, life events) is the problem: is the response adaptation or sensitisation (10), freezing rather than fight-or-flight (11), driven by perception more than the stressor (15)? Inference: items 5 and 10 argue for individual, revised plans rather than a fixed team routine.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — The list cites no studies; items 7 and 16-18 (the "superconscious," Jung's types, a "seldom-tapped source of energy") are speculative and outside sport science as practised. Item 1 ("any technique will work ... if you believe in it") overstates the placebo point the authors make more carefully on PDF 455-456, and item 9 qualifies item 8 on the same page. Treat the list as the authors' views, not findings.
    28	
    29	**Example** — Item 15 in the authors' own words: "alteration of our perceptions and thoughts may manage the stress effectively," and "our perception or assessment of the attractiveness or repulsiveness of the stressor can alter our belief that the stressor can be managed" (PDF 467 / p.456).
    30	
    31	**Related** — [[principle--find-the-optimum-stress-level-rather-than-avoiding-stress]], [[claim--placebo-and-therapist-rapport-carry-much-of-restoration-effect]], [[principle--train-athletes-to-cope-with-perceived-as-well-as-actual-load]], [[heuristic--arousal-optimum-is-individual-so-fit-restoration-to-personality-and-task-complexity]]

6:chapter: "8.2"
14:# Physical Training Must Prepare Tendons, Ligaments and Bone as Well as Muscle, With Heavy or Rapid Loads Playing a Valuable Role
--- 33
- The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)**
--- 40
- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
--- 74
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
--- 89
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
--- 102
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
--- 104
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
--- 109
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]
--- 142
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
--- 151
- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
--- 153
- Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)**
--- 187
- Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17): "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)**

- **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric stated or claimed the position in the interview. His words are quoted as "Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Qn):". Q1 claimed exactly four course positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system priority stack); other course material stays Inferred.
- **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric said the source or practice is not current. The old content is kept and marked, not deleted, so a synthesis note can see what changed.
- **Superseded by interview (Qn)**: a documented position, sometimes from Eric's own slides, that his interview answer replaces.

- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
--- 109
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]
--- 142
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
--- 151
- Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
--- 153
- Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)**

- Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17): "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)**

15:# Overtraining From Too Much Volume Versus Too Much Intensity, as Printed (Slide 9)
17:**What it is** — Slide 9: "Strength training athletes are prone to overtraining from too much volume (addisonic-sympathetic inhibition)-which usually occurs in endurance athletes and from too much intensity (basedowic-sympathetic over activity)." The slide credits its list to Wendler's article (see [[framework--reasons-for-deloading-rest-the-mind-overtraining-injury-and-progress]]); it does not say whether the volume and intensity sentence is Wendler's. The slide also says "Christian Thibaudeau articles on T-nation detail this more and is a great source of info." It also says "Prevent overtraining-yes Joe Weider & the barbarian brothers there is such a thing." Presenter unconfirmed: the deck prints no author, venue or date, and the PDF metadata author field ("David  Tate") is not used for identity; see _book.md.
19:**Why it works** — The deck gives no mechanism and defines neither term. Inference: "sympathetic inhibition" for volume and "sympathetic over activity" for intensity map to a parasympathetic-dominant and a sympathetic-dominant picture of overtraining, as the Samuels deck in this library describes them, but the slide does not say so.

5:book: overtraining-and-sleep--samuels
7:topic: two clinical pictures of overtraining syndrome, with sleep disturbance in only one
8:category: [overtraining, overtraining-syndrome, sympathetic, parasympathetic, sleep, slide-deck]
14:# Overtraining Syndrome Is Split Into a Sympathetic Type With Disturbed Sleep and a Parasympathetic Type Without
16:**What it is** — PDF p.26, "Overtraining Syndrome", is a two-column list credited on the slide to Kreider, Fry and O'Toole (eds), Overtraining in Sport, Human Kinetics, 1998, p.21. Both types share impaired performance and lack of supercompensation. The Sympathetic Type adds restlessness and irritability, disturbed sleep, weight loss, increased resting heart rate, increased resting blood pressure, and retarded recovery after exercise (8 items in all). The Parasympathetic Type adds fatigue, depression and apathy (slide: "apathia"); "Not sleep disturbed"; constant weight; low resting heart rate; low resting blood pressure; suppressed heart-rate, glucose and lactate exercise profiles; suppressed neuromuscular excitability; suppressed sympathetic intrinsic activity; suppressed catecholamine sensitivity; and altered hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal/gonadal function (14 items in all).
18:**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism on this slide and no explanation of what the two type names mean. Inference: the table separates the types by autonomic direction (raised resting heart rate and blood pressure in one, lowered in the other), but the deck does not say so.
20:**When to apply** — Inference: as the deck's own limit on a sleep-based screen. Samuels's p.26 list has disturbed sleep in the sympathetic type and "not sleep disturbed" in the parasympathetic type, so an athlete in the second picture would not be flagged by a sleep complaint. Evans p.17 lists increased sleeping for this type, so a question about amount of sleep might still catch it. The deck does not draw this point in the pages read. Eric's baseline: Eric keeps no formal risk model (`method-baseline.md`, Q12, Explicit) and has the coach's eye flag where to look and data then investigate (Q6, Explicit); the baseline does not mention resting heart rate or blood pressure, though Polar heart rate is in the technology stack (`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting", Explicit).
26:**Related** — [[elite-sports-performance--evans/claim--sympathetic-vs-parasympathetic-overtraining-and-omegawave-readiness-case]] (the two-type split agrees. Details differ: Evans p.17 puts depression in the sympathetic type too ("increased irritability and depression"), Evans p.17 and p.18 have fatigue in both types, and Evans p.17 has increased sleeping in the parasympathetic type against Samuels's "Not sleep disturbed", while Evans p.18 gives normal sleep for that type. Evans also assigns the sympathetic type to team, strength and power sports and the parasympathetic type to endurance sports; Samuels does not. Neither source gives data, and Evans's tables carry no named source. Inference: these are differences between symptom lists from unsourced tables, not opposite claims about the same finding, so confidence stays `untested`), [[framework--adaptive-versus-maladaptive-training-overload-curves]], [[claim--a-sleep-history-belongs-in-overtraining-screening]].

14:# Overtraining Syndrome Is Split Into a Sympathetic Type With Disturbed Sleep and a Parasympathetic Type Without
16:**What it is** — PDF p.26, "Overtraining Syndrome", is a two-column list credited on the slide to Kreider, Fry and O'Toole (eds), Overtraining in Sport, Human Kinetics, 1998, p.21. Both types share impaired performance and lack of supercompensation. The Sympathetic Type adds restlessness and irritability, disturbed sleep, weight loss, increased resting heart rate, increased resting blood pressure, and retarded recovery after exercise (8 items in all). The Parasympathetic Type adds fatigue, depression and apathy (slide: "apathia"); "Not sleep disturbed"; constant weight; low resting heart rate; low resting blood pressure; suppressed heart-rate, glucose and lactate exercise profiles; suppressed neuromuscular excitability; suppressed sympathetic intrinsic activity; suppressed catecholamine sensitivity; and altered hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal/gonadal function (14 items in all).
18:**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism on this slide and no explanation of what the two type names mean. Inference: the table separates the types by autonomic direction (raised resting heart rate and blood pressure in one, lowered in the other), but the deck does not say so.
20:**When to apply** — Inference: as the deck's own limit on a sleep-based screen. Samuels's p.26 list has disturbed sleep in the sympathetic type and "not sleep disturbed" in the parasympathetic type, so an athlete in the second picture would not be flagged by a sleep complaint. Evans p.17 lists increased sleeping for this type, so a question about amount of sleep might still catch it. The deck does not draw this point in the pages read. Eric's baseline: Eric keeps no formal risk model (`method-baseline.md`, Q12, Explicit) and has the coach's eye flag where to look and data then investigate (Q6, Explicit); the baseline does not mention resting heart rate or blood pressure, though Polar heart rate is in the technology stack (`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting", Explicit).

In the dynamometer and tonometer rows all three groups rise under squeezing, kneading and percussion, and fall or stay flat under stroking. 14. `claim--manual-massage-raises-blood-flow-while-high-frequency-vibromassage-lowers-it.md`, frontmatter `confidence: supported` against "When NOT to apply", "The studies are cited, not described". The brief requires the named study to be described in the book for `supported`. Dubrovsky's method is partly described (radioactive Xenon markers, myotonometry); Burovykh et al is not. ## Missing ideas (content on PDF 444-467 with no entry)

Count: 5. The three most important:

1. **Three phases of normal recovery** (Zalessky, 1979; PDF 455 / p.444): on-going (during activity), rapid (immediately after; by-product removal and energy replenishment), delayed ("surpasses the initial level if training loads are not excessive"). Quoted only as context inside the Talyshev case study; it is the frame the timing rules rest on.
2. **Deeper workout fatigue gives larger after-effects and a stronger recovery flow, provided loads are carefully prescribed; Talyshev's two sides of recovery** (PDF 460 / p.449): immediate, most complete recovery (e.g. during competition) versus recovery in daily training to raise work capacity. This underpins both the timing heuristic and the blunting warning.
3. **Goal-directed episodes of inaction** (PDF 455 / p.444): Western athletes copy multi-session Soviet programmes "religiously" but ignore "the contents and structure of the phases between training exercises and sessions"; planned inaction is not appreciated.

(The other two: "Individualisation of approach is vital, as is variation, though not simply for the sake of it" (PDF 455); the practitioner Code of Conduct and duty to refer to someone more qualified (PDF 460), only touched in the massage entry.)
